utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, and good morning, Mr. Stojanovic. May we thank you for coming back. There was one matter that was overlooked while you were here. Mr. Re. If I could remind you that the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again, I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Further cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, good morning, and I apologise to you for having brought you back. It was my oversight forgetting to ask you several specific questions about the specific area yesterday, and I thank you for coming back. In your evidence on -- two days ago, Mr. Petrovic asked you about discipline within the 472nd Brigade. And you said "in my company, I believe the discipline was at the required level. That is to say, in accordance with the tasks we received from our superiors." I'm just saying this to remind you of your evidence. Next question was: "What about fire discipline within your company?" Your answer was: Well, let me tell you, we are professionals, and we respect the orders of our superior officers. So there could not be any opening of fire without dire necessity." First of all, do you remember giving those -- do you remember those questions and answers to Mr. Petrovic on Monday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer said it was in your company you believe the discipline was at the required level. Were you referring to your own specific company within the 472nd, and were you confining it to that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to my company specifically, that is the unit which I was commander, the 3rd Motorised Company of the 3rd Motorised Brigade. According to the regulations then in force in the then JNA, now the Army of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, I, as commander of a unit, have the right to provide conclusions concerning order, work, and discipline only as concerns my unit, the unit that I am in charge of. I am not entitled to pass my opinion on any other units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you're not entitled to pass, in your words, your opinion on other units, you were aware that in the period of October, November, and December 1991 there were discipline problems within the 472nd, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, can you please only ask me questions about the 3rd Motorised Battalion because that was my unit and about my company. I'm not aware of what was going on in the rest of the brigade. You'll have to go and ask someone who was a member of the brigade back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence is that you were operating in the Bosanka area. Now, there was an incident involving soldiers of the 472nd on about the 30th of October 1991. There was a firing of a machine-gun from the Golobov Kamen firing position on that day, unauthorised. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The time period that you are talking about, at that time the 3rd Company of the 3rd Motorised Battalion, unit of which I was commander, was not there at the time. At that time we had been pulled out to the village of Talez where, as company commander, I organised for my units to rest. And I had been sent home on sick leave because I had pneumonia. Therefore, I can't really provide a specific answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Zec issued an order in relation to the looting of houses in Osojnik and Ivanica on that day for members of the 472nd. Were you aware that there had been incidents of looting in Osojnik and Ivanica, end of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the interpretation is Captain Zec. It wasn't Captain Zec. It was Warship Captain Zec. There is a major difference there in terms of military chain of command and ranks. As to your question, the answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P108. And also P107.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to have a look at the two documents, please, Mr. Stojanovic. That's firstly an order of Admiral Jokic of the 31st of October, and secondly the order of Warship Captain Zec of the same date.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first document that I've seen that was signed by chief of staff of the 9th VPS, Warship Captain Zec. This is a period of time when my unit was not in those positions, but rather was resting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having -- just go back to the first one, from your knowledge of the operation of the JNA and military hierarchy, the incidents as complained of would have to be fairly serious for someone of Zec's seniority to issue such an order, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. In the JNA, an order to improve order and discipline is issued from all levels of command from an independent unit command up to the very highest level of all. Therefore, this sort of order to improve order and discipline is a perfectly usual thing. It could be issued by an independent unit commander, a platoon commander, a company commander, or, as in the case of Mr. Zec, the chief of staff of the sector command. That makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular order refers to some very specific incidences of indiscipline by members of a named brigade. This shows, doesn't it, a level of concern, or grave concern by the command of the 9th VPS about indiscipline within the 472nd?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not sure which unnamed brigade you are talking about. I can't speak about any unnamed units because there was no such unit in the JNA. Each man at his own level of command regulates and carries out orders given by their superiors that have to do with order and discipline. What you've shown me, this document, I can't see anything that could provide clues to me to answer your question, whether this was really like this or not. You'll have to ask someone who was actually in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you, sir, about the attitude of the writer. It shows, doesn't it, that the person on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection because the witness can't speak about the attitude of the writer, of the author of this document that he is being presented with. The writer's attitude is something that witness can in no way be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That effectively forecloses that question, Mr. Re. It isn't a criticism of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way this is written is expressed in such a way as to convey concern from the command of the 9th VPS about indiscipline, isn't it? I'm just talking about the way it's expressed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, you'll have to ask the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector, or possibly his deputy, Zec, if there was any concern felt by them concerning order and discipline. You can't be asking me whether he had any concerns about this. He was the commander. It was up to him to call those shots. My level of command was my company. I really can't go into the substance of these documents you're showing me. These documents never reached me. In terms of the chain of command they were never supposed to reach me. I was never supposed to see these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a very experienced officer. Had you received this letter, you would have been very concerned to be notified about these sorts of incidents of indiscipline within the ranks, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday and the day before yesterday, in my unit, the 3rd Company of the 3rd Motorised Battalion, I made sure there was complete order, that the work was being done, and there was discipline. I can't talk about anything else because I can't speculate. I can't base my answers on assumptions. These are some theoretical matters that are studied at military schools. My experience back then was that of a company commander. I do happen to have a higher rank now, but that has got nothing to do with the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the incidents described there, they are serious incidents of indiscipline, if correct, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was down to the officers to think about those things or in whoever's unit that was happening. This was not the case in my unit, therefore there was no reason for me to be concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about this. I'm asking you to look at what is described there. That is the unnecessary opening of machine-gun fire and the looting of houses. If true, as a military officer, these are very serious breaches of discipline and criminal offences, aren't they? Don't worry about what happened in your command. I'm not asking you. I'm asking you about what is described there. Those are very serious breaches, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first of all I do not know at all that this was indeed the case. If I don't know that, and if none of this ever happened in my unit, then I would be hard put to think about what someone else may or may not have done. That's their problem. They're in charge of their own units. And if this happened in someone else's unit, they would have to bear the responsibility for that. It has got nothing to do with me. How should I be saying -- what should I be telling you now about what discipline should be across army units? I think it's asking too much of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that issue of indiscipline, your answer two days ago, you said there could not be any opening of fire without dire necessity. The opening of -- unauthorised opening of machine-gun --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it's a proper question. Be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit is being misquoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Be seated, please. I was very disturbed with your interjection earlier which gave the witness a very clear witness. That's why I'm very impatient with you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you will be drawing to a close shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Very, very shortly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the unauthorised opening of machine-gun fire without dire necessity would be a breach of discipline, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who it was that opened fire from machine-gun. Which machine-gun is it you're referring to? Why didn't you refer to a rifle or whatever, machine-gun? Which machine-gun are we talking about and who was it who was opening fire from that machine-gun? I'm afraid I don't understand your question at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on that issue of firepower, just to clarify something, did your unit have 82-millimetre mortars in the Bosanka area on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit, the unit of which I was commander, did not have 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware whether the units at Strincijera had 82-millimetre --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please may I address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Cautiously, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes without saying, Your Honour. I understood, although I was not present at the time, when the ruling was made to recall this witness that this ruling referred to one single question, a particular question, the question of discipline. And now my learned colleague is reopening the cross-examination without your permission, without your explicit authorisation. I think that is the way he's headed right now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If he went much further, your comment would be justified, Mr. Petrovic. He's right on the edge now, as I think he knows. Carry on, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. It is indeed my last question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware whether the units at Strincijera had 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any further re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thank you once again for your assistance. You're now free to go. And I believe we will not have to trouble you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the next witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Petrovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Yesterday, in answer to one of my questions, you described that you left the Bosanka village area and that you left for Srdj pursuant to orders you had received from your superior command. Sir, can you tell us if at one point in time you, in fact, arrived at the Srdj feature?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I arrived at the very top of the Srdj feature where the repeater is, at the highest point of the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along the way, did you come under fire at any point?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came under fire, as I said before, when we set out, and then after we had gone more than half the way, and then having reached the Srdj feature itself, my men and I came under fire from the facilities and buildings that are on the hilltop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which side did you approach the Srdj feature from?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the side of the town and along a bend in the road. There's a slope going down towards the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time did you reach the feature?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, just before 8.00. That's when we reached the feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to a tank yesterday. As you were advancing from the village of Bosanka up towards Srdj, was this tank used to open fire?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the tank opened fire at the Srdj feature on several occasions. I think it must have fired at least three or four shells before we actually reached the feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, sir, as to tell us when this tank was attached to your unit, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the company was reinforced with this tank in early December that same year, which is to say a few days before the attack on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, sir, can you please describe what happened once you reached the repeater?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After reaching the Srdj feature itself, several hundred metres further up, I used my radio communications to stop the firing preparation and to ask the mortars to stop firing at the feature so I could continue the attack. Then not having carried out any special preparations, we actually entered the facility up there. Having reached the feature, there was the infantry combat, hand-to-hand combat with the Croatian forces at the feature. This was close-range fighting using automatic rifles and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hand grenades. After about half an hour of fighting, I was wounded at the very top of Srdj, a stone's throw from the repeater itself. I was hit by shrapnel from a hand grenade to the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that in due course. Did you call on the crew up at the Srdj feature to surrender, having reached the positions around the antenna?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group had a megaphone, and having reached the Srdj feature and having taken control of the Srdj feature, I used the megaphone repeatedly to call on the forces that were defending Srdj because we had taken control of the area that were deep inside the tunnels within the feature itself. And I called on them to surrender. I had this megaphone. I called on the forces to surrender, and that was the reason I brought the megaphone along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that among other equipment you had AGF grenades. Just take it slowly that my question and your answer can be properly recorded. You had these AGF grenades. Did you use them?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After calling them to surrender and receiving no answer from the Croatian fighters in the tunnels below Srdj, I used two AGF grenades throwing them into the opening leading to the depth -- into the depth of that facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the use of this equipment have any effect?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, no, because the system of tunnels below this building is such that draft helped release the smoke immediately, as I could see myself as soon as I threw the grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at one point you were wounded. Describe it, please, what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I emerged near the building in the vicinity of the repeater and after capturing the repeater on top of Srdj, there was something in the form of a cube erected on stop of Srdj, 5 metres high with stairs leading to it. There was an entrance there leading into the ground, leading underground, according to our information which was not necessarily correct, there were three storeys underground. I called them to surrender. I said if they surrender, we would not hurt them. However, they started throwing hand grenades out of that opening. There were six or seven of my men on that plateau up there from the moment the grenades were thrown in we had about two seconds' time to move away to avoid consequences. At one point, I turned sideways so as to move a part of my men forward because we were grouped together in that area. And if I remember correctly, the seventh grenade that had been thrown out of that tunnel fell about half a metre to a metre away from my left shoulder. I had no time to remove the grenade. I only had time to turn sideways. The grenade exploded, and a part of it hit my head. It actually hit my helmet, pierced it, and I was hit in the nape of my neck on the left side of my head. Two shrapnel remained in my bulletproof jacket, and other shrapnel remained in a discarded fridge that was nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 8.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took over command after you were wounded near the repeater?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After being wounded, I established contact with my battalion commander, told him that I was wounded, that I needed replacement. And my group was taken over by a second -- by a junior sergeant, Tuka Miralem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if some senior officer took over command over the Srdj group later?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that company commander, Captain Stojanovic, came to this group on Srdj and commanded the forces until they were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you pulled out of that area?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to attempt to descend on my own, helped by two of my soldiers. There was a Pinzgauer on the way to pick me up. I got into it. It happened -- it was happening all between Bosanka and Srdj. And then I handed over command to Tuka Miralem, junior sergeant, and then I withdrew to the area of Bosanka where I received medical assistance. My wound was cauterised, and then I was transferred to a medical facility in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the hospital, or how long did you receive treatment?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed about three or four days in the hospital at Trebinje, and after that, my treatment continued at home. And I returned to my unit in end December approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, concerning these events and the attack on Mount Srdj, did anybody in your platoon, your company, or your battalion receive any commendation to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody in your platoon, company, or battalion receive promotion or decoration for this action?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my platoon certainly, and I have no knowledge about the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe the commander of your company was promoted or decorated for the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a delegation of generals, generals visiting the area of Zarkovica, Bosanka, Strincijera, the positions of the 3rd Battalion after the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 6th of December, I already said I spent around 20 days receiving treatment at hospital and at home. And after that, I didn't see any visit of any generals or anybody else in the Zarkovica or any other of those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Pesic: Did you at any point receive an official grade or assessment or evaluation for your work in the unit of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion for the period you spent in that unit?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was evaluated for the period of 1991, 1992, that is, from the moment when I transferred to another unit until I left it. My evaluation was written sometime in May 1992. And my evaluation said "exceptional performance."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what period does this evaluation relate?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1991 to May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that official evaluation that said "exceptional performance"?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalion commander Vladimir Kovacevic. However, this evaluation, exceptional performance, has to be confirmed by a superior officer, and therefore this endorsement was given by Captain of Frigate, Kovacevic -- sorry, Zec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you get this evaluation, exceptional performance, who has to confirm it?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom, you have a line that says "I agree with the evaluation, Captain of Warship Zec," because it was he who was in command of that naval sector at the time when I was evaluated after Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Philip Weiner, and I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. Won't be that long. Now, sir, you testified you took part in military action on December 6th, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us how you were injured and hospitalised. Did anyone interview you as to the events of December 6th while you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon of the 6th when I was already at the hospital, I was visited by some of my soldiers who took part together with me in this action, people who were part of my assault group, and I learned from them what happened later at that facility after I was wounded and taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from the 2nd Operational Group ever interview you concerning your activities and what you observed on the 6th of December 1991? Anyone in the 2nd Operational Group command?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever contacted and asked to report to the 2nd Operational Group command to be interviewed concerning the events of December 6th?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever ordered to file a report as to your observations and activities on December 6th with the 2nd Operational Group command?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never told to do anything of the kind, and I never wrote a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever hear of anyone being investigated by the JNA as a result of their actions on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I returned, I heard that one commanding officer had written some sort of statement, but I never heard that any sort of proceedings had been instituted or that anybody was held responsible, at least out of the commanders in the battalion. Nothing like that was initiated by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of any -- that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was shelled on that date, on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was on the axis of attack towards Srdj. The town was behind me. So that during the action, I was unable to observe what was going on in my rear, especially since I was wounded and pulled out for treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, did you ever hear of anyone being investigated, prosecuted in a military or civilian court, or punished for the shelling of the Old Town on December 6th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. You testified that you took part in the combat operations in November of 1991. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in November of 1991, that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was shelled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the positions in the area of Zarkovica, I arrived on the 9th in the evening. I knew that for several days previously, combat operations had been going on to take Zarkovica and Bosanka, but I didn't know that anybody -- what was going on exactly because I arrived several days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were also unaware that boats and vessels in the Old Town harbour had been shelled by the JNA as well as the walls or ramparts of the Old Town? You weren't aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on television, Croatian radio and television, footage of some vessels in the marina burning, but I did not see it with my own eyes. I know only what I saw on television or things that I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And had you ever heard of any investigation by the 2nd Operational Group in relation to that shelling in November of the Old Town? Were you aware of any investigation, or did you hear of any investigation after that shelling?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I learned while I was in the area of Dubrovnik has to do with the command of the 9th Naval Sector. And at that time, in view of my rank and position, I was not aware of the existence of any other operations groups, so I was unable to hear of any investigation targeting commanding officers or anyone in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you hadn't -- you weren't aware of any investigation. Obviously, would you agree that you weren't aware of anyone being punished or prosecuted in a military or civilian court as a result of a November shelling either? You weren't aware of any officer being punished or prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that you left Bosanka and proceeded towards Srdj, as you did this morning, too. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went with a tank and 12 to 14 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you were fired upon early as you left Bosanka, halfway, and then when you're on top of Srdj you were fired upon by Croatian mortars. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire from Croatian mortars was opened when I was two-thirds of the way towards Srdj. When I came close, the fire stopped. And when I arrived there, fire was reopened from both infantry weapons and mortars so that there was no fire from mortars at the time when I was taking over that facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw mortars firing from the area of Babin Kuk. You said the tennis courts. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see those mortars firing from the area when you were two-thirds away, or did you see it when you were on top of Srdj? When did you see those mortars firing?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately halfway towards Srdj. The observer who was to the left on the edge, topographically speaking reported that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the observer reported it. Did you see with your own eyes the firing from that area?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I could see it with my own eyes, after the fire was opened and after I received report from the observer. I saw through my binoculars in the area of the woods two pieces from which fire had been opened. I could see the smoke and I could see the fire at the opening of the barrel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of the distance between Srdj and Babin Kuk, you had to use binoculars; you couldn't see from that distance with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you know it was several kilometres away, Babin Kuk, from Srdj?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, about 2 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to see something, see more tars from 2 kilometres away, you have to use binoculars to see a mortar?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you can't see with the naked eye, obviously, from that distance?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that distance, fire can be seen that is coming out of a barrel. But it can be seen better, more precisely, through binoculars. However, fire can be seen even with the naked eye. Since it's about 6.30 only, it hasn't even dawned properly, so the flash coming from the muzzle can be seen even with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that distance of approximately 2 kilometres, to see the mortar itself, the apparatus, you have to use binoculars. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you thought it was 82-millimetre mortars. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was only through using -- well, you know first there are different sizes of mortars? You know that, sir? There's 82, there's 120--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. They could not understand your answer. Could you please repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were different calibres of mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that distance, it's difficult to determine the calibre, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, as a professional soldier, the range, distance is sufficient for. For me, it is sufficient to see the crater that is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. result of the explosion, and then I can tell what the calibre was. I'm sure that they were 81 or 82 millimetres depending on the weapon used. There were both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from looking from that distance, you really can't determine the size of the mortar; you had to look at the actual crater that was created by the shell exploding in order to determine the calibre because you're that far away. Is that correct? Even with binoculars, you're still that far away?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I looked through the binoculars and on the basis of the crater that I saw, and I would like to note that between 20 and 30 shells were fired at us in that period of time, I established that these were 81 or 82-millimetre mortars. So I can explain. 60-millimetre mortars --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm saying is: From that distance, you couldn't even with binoculars alone make that determination; you had to look at the crater size because of that distance of 2 kilometres away. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what finally convinced me that those were the weapons concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just one last area of questioning: You indicated that while you were coming under fire yesterday you indicated that you asked for support, you asked for -- and they said that Babin Kuk was out of range of the 120-millimetre mortars on Uskoplje. Is that correct? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware, sir, that the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade had 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my battalion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade under Miroslav Jovanovic, commander. Were you aware that they had 120-millimetre mortars in the area of Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is outside my area. So I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware that the 120-millimetre mortars on Mokosica or the 3rd Battalion of the 5th did, in fact, fire upon Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I took part in the fighting in Srdj, before my wounding, the area of Babin Kuk was not fired at. And what unit was on the other side where Mokosica is is something I don't know or I didn't know because I was a platoon commander. I did not know about that because it was too far away from the positions taken by my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit D65, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at page 2. Do you see on page 2 that long paragraph in the B/C/S, in the Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian? Do you see halfway down on the right side the first command "commandant 3/5 pmtbr"? Do you see that, where it says ... Do you see that where it says "considering that our forces at Srdj were in the clearing, the commander of the 3rd/472nd pmtbr directly requested support of the 3/5th, the 3rd" - basically - "Battalion of the 5th at 7.30 hours?" Do you see that, sir? And it says "from 7.45 to 8.30 hours and later from 9.10 to 11.15 hours the commander of the 3rd of the 5th pmtbr fired on the mortar positions on the ZNG in the regions of Lazaret, Hotel Neptune, Nuncijata, Sustjepan, Hotel Petka, Babin Kuk, Libertas, that is all targets outside the Old Town"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 120-millimetre mortars did in fact fire upon that area in Babin Kuk? Although you weren't aware of it, they did in fact fire upon the Croatian borders in Babin Kuk, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I asked for support I could not get support. At the time mentioned here, the 120-millimetre mortars from Mokosica were firing at Babin Kuk, I was either at Srdj itself in close-range infantry fighting, so I did not have time to observe what was going on behind me. As for the second opening of fire, I was already en route to hospital in Trebinje by then. So at the moment when I asked for fire support, when I was first shot at by mortars from that area, I was told that they were not within the range of our weapons in Uskoplje. And later on, I couldn't observe anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm saying is: JNA mortars did, in fact, fire upon that area according to that document, which is an official JNA document. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a moment, please. Re-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. Pesic, did anybody from the VPS ask you for a statement or ask you about what happened on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that upon arriving in the unit you were at Zarkovica -- or rather, that you came and that you were in the area of Zarkovica. And my learned friend asked you about what can be seen at a 2.000-metre distance. That was more or less the wording that my learned friend used. So, from Zarkovica, which is 2.000 metres away from the Old Town, what can be seen there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no discussion of Zarkovica. This man went from Bosanka to Srdj, and from Srdj and Bosanka, looked upon Babin Kuk. There was no discussion of Zarkovica in my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the month of November, that's what he said. The essence of my question, Your Honour, pertains to what can be seen at a 2.000-metre distance. That is what my learned friend asked, and with your permission, that is what I want to ask the witness. What can be seen at a 2.000-metre distance? So the point is the distance, not the actual position, regardless of whether it's Zarkovica or whatever. So, of course, if you give me permission to ask that, I will. If you do not, I will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you go about asking that in relation to what was seen at Babin Kuk that day, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, at a distance of 2.000 metres, can you distinguish a human figure?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a human figure can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see a human figure at a 2.000-metre distance without binoculars, without an artillery compass, without any other tools?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A human figure can be seen, particularly because the town that was being observed is at a much lower altitude than the facility where we were. So it is much easier to see the -- a human figure and dark and light colours and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a 2.000-metre distance, can one discern with the naked eye whether one sees a man, a grown man, or a child?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that situation, that specific situation, when our positions were higher up in relation to the Old Town and everything that was being observed, a person with good eyesight could tell whether it was an adult, a grown man, or a child that could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no further proposals. And with regard to this subject, we are going to put forth other matters when the time comes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Pesic, we must thank you, indeed, for the assistance you've given for the Tribunal and for coming here to give evidence. You'll be pleased to know you're now free to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you agree, could we please have the first morning break now because the next witness has just arrived, so perhaps this would be a good moment to take the first morning break, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 5 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read the affirmation from the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please introduce yourself by your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm Dr. Miodrag Soc. I was born on the 1st of September 1959 in Podgorica, Montenegro, where I still live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please tell us what you do today and where you work.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I work in Podgorica at the clinical centre of Montenegro which is the leading system -- which is a leading institution in the health system of Montenegro. I am an expert in forensic medicine, and I also teach. I'm a professor at the faculty of medicine, the only one in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you kindly to pause before giving your answer because all of this needs to be interpreted. Tell me, please, what has been your education?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course, I completed elementary school and high school in Podgorica. Then I graduated from the school of medicine in Zagreb at the University of Zagreb. On the 7th of February 1987 I graduated. Then I completed my graduate studies also at the University in Zagreb. I got my masters degree in December 1992 in Belgrade because war had broken out in the meantime. In 1998, on the 16th of July, I became a doctor of sciences, also in Belgrade. On the 4th of September, I passed my specialist examination, and since then I have been a specialist in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Doctor, are you a member of any associations? Do you hold a position in any such association?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Association of Forensic Medicine of Montenegro. I am a member of the Presidency of the Association for Forensic Medicine of Serbia Montenegro. I'm a member of the Association of Court Experts of Serbia Montenegro for forensic medicine. And also, and I am a member of the Association for Forensic Medicine of southeast Europe, or rather the Balkans, and this is being established now under the leadership of Professor Aleksai Duma who is a professor in Skopje, Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Doctor, did you write any papers and books, and did you publish them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course. That is compulsory, if a doctor is to develop professionally. Until now, I have published over 40 papers, about 30 of them were written by me only. And I also wrote many articles. In 2000, I wrote a book in the field of forensic medicine and traffic and transportation which is the most frequent cause of death in my country, or rather, in my republic. Traffic accidents, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, have you given an expert opinion regarding the medical documentation of General Strugar, and for this particular case, and were these documents submitted to you by the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, I studied these medical documents which consists of records of dead bodies that were examined on the 19th of December 1991. This consists of the medical documents of Valjalo Mato and Vlasica Ivo. Those are the two persons whose medical documents these are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, when you mentioned the date of the external examination, the date here is the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, that's not the date. I see that it's a mistake. And perhaps I should wait for the interpretation. No, it's not the 19th of December. It is the 7th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, did you study the record of external examinations of dead bodies dated the 7th of December 1991 that is registered as an exhibit in this trial, and it's number is P70?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at these documents in detail. I studied them in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the point of view of the rules that you apply in your field, this record of external examinations of dead bodies, was it put together in compliance with those same rules?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: My opinion is that the rules were not complied with, the rules of forensic medicine, namely, which is a science.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please show this expert witness Prosecution Exhibit P70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please tell me: If you look at the external examination of a dead body, do you include a description of wounds in that sort of report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: When you carry out an external examination, all changes must be described, and so must wounds. All changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what was done in this record on the external examination of dead bodies dated the 7th of December, which is Exhibit P70? Is that how it was done in compliance with the rules applied by those who practice forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I think not because a good -- the less parameters have been used for description than you normally should use when carrying out an external examination. In the literature that I've studied, it says that when you describe a dead body during an external examination, there must be at least 19 parameters. Women have 20 because there is a description of breast. So there are at least 19 or 20 parameters, plus the injuries that are also described in addition to those. Here, we only find five or six parameters being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please tell us what an autopsy is, the technical definition.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: According to the medical definition, an autopsy or a postmortem - these are synonyms - that is, the opening of the abdominal cavity and the analysis of internal organs, and this is used to establish the cause and the mechanism that brought about death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please tell us how many different kinds of autopsy are there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The fundamental breakdown is pathological, anatomical, and forensic autopsy. Those kinds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in essence what is the difference between forensic medical autopsy on the one hand and the pathological and anatomical autopsy on the other?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: There are substantial differences. The main difference is that with the pathological and anatomical autopsy which is sometimes referred to as clinical autopsy, you don't take into account the external examination of a body. And the answer is always provided only as to the cause of death. When you have a forensic medical autopsy, it is important to study and describe in detail all the external changes on a body which you find during an external examination. And you provide answers as to the mechanism of death. Therefore, it is a sort of synergy, the forensic medical autopsy, and thus is a more complex form of autopsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you studied the record of the external examination of dead bodies marked as P70, with each individual body that was examined, at the end of the description, the cause of death was given, too. These causes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of death, as given, are they medically correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, of course I did read that, and I saw that at the end of the description. After the bodies were examined, the cause of death was given. These causes of death as given were for the main part misspelled or wrongly given because it was obvious that an explosive wound had caused death. Sometimes an explosive wound with haemorrhage, and medically it is clear that an explosive wound or injury cannot cause death. It can only be the mechanism by which death comes about. But it cannot be the cause of death. So in purely medical terms, I think this is false.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Doctor, an explosive wound as a cause of death according to the rules of your science cannot be given as such in a record of the external examination of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course an explosion, or rather, fragments of an explosive device cannot be agents of death. There can be hemorrhaging. There can be a shock. But certainly, those two cannot be confused. Mechanism of death is one thing, and cause of death is another. So this is an error. You can't give such a diagnose, death caused by an explosive injury or wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you look at P70, the exhibit, if you look at all of the 19 cases where bodies were examined, can you see anywhere whether the person who performed the autopsy, in fact, reconstructed the injuries such as they occurred? Did they perhaps -- did they alter the injuries in terms of how wide or how deep the injuries were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: When I studied the medical files, I did not notice that any of the wounds were reconstructed, that the wounds were cut up or widened, any wounds or injuries. Not in any of the cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would mean, Doctor, wouldn't it, that this record of external examination contains no such descriptions, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Not that I found any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's assume that the pathologist who performed the autopsy, the autopsy -- who reconstructed the wounds, by cutting, expanding, or deepening them in compliance with the rules of your field when performing an autopsy, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: First of all, you don't do it. If do you it, this would amount to a desecration of the body. Primary findings are never to be altered. They must be established, described in detail, and then an opinion is provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let us assume that the pathologist violated the rules usually applied during an autopsy. If he had reconstructed the wounds by cutting, widening, or deepening the existing wounds on a body, would he not have to describe these actions in his written finding?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, you must state that. You must state any additional action that was taken. Sometimes, but only sometimes, you take alcohol or rather blood from the veins in the leg, but this must be reflected in the record, from the deep veins. Everything that is done must be entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if, for example, an investigating judge issues an order to the pathologist to carry out an external examination of dead bodies, in that case, does one open and cut up any parts of the body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: By no means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your field, the pathologist in P70, in Exhibit P70, did he comply with the rules of forensic medicine or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I think I mentioned in my expert opinion that I had found certain errors. Some of the errors have to do with the fact that too few parameters were established by external examination. I'm not sure if this can be interpreted as an error or not. But certain remarks that were made during the examination in terms of establishing the amount of blood within the abdominal cavity, I think the estimates were a bit too liberal or too descriptive. There seems to have been a lot of blood. Within the rules of service, you must open the abdominal cavity, you must measure exactly the amount of blood that is in there, the colour of blood, and its consistency. You don't even call it blood. You say "contents." Because at the time an autopsy is performed, the pathologist does not know what substance he is looking at. It can be mixed with gunpowder or something like that, for example. So I think this is another example of errors that were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please look at P70 and look at number 5. It is a dead body of an unidentified male person.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Very well. I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this description, did the pathologist establish that there was an extraneous body at the back of the upper arm?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The examining doctor described that there was some shrapnel, small shrapnel there. However, the description of this foreign body is not satisfactory. If you find a foreign body there during an examination, or autopsy of the body, it must be extracted, that is taken out. Must be described fully and measured. And these parameters must then, of course, be recorded, which we don't find in this case. All we have is "a small piece of shrapnel."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you look at the same document, P70, number 15, if you look at this description, that is the external examination under 15 of the body of Pavo Urban, do we find there a description of any widening of the wound or reconstruction of the wound based on what we find in the record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, there is no such description. What it states is that around the stomach, an explosive wound was found of an irregular shape, about 5 centimetres in diameter. The edges of the wound are described, and there is a liberal description of blood in the abdominal cavity. And I've already pointed out that it can't be done like this. So this description that you've referred to is not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, from this record, item 15, can we see if any foreign body had been found and located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, there is no description of any foreign body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the pathologist in question had found a foreign body such as a shrapnel, would he have been required to describe it in the record, including the location where it was found and its description, what exactly it was and what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I have already said that when identifying a foreign body during postmortem, this foreign body is extracted and has to be described. It is described very basically, including the colour, the form, the size, if there is no exact measuring instrument, at least the diameter is given in millimetres. And later, if the postmortem hall is not well-equipped enough, it has to be measured exactly, such as descriptions that we do with projectiles of up to three decimal points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, when you look at this record on external examination of bodies, Exhibit P70, item 11, this is the external examination of the body of Tonci Skocko. The description mentioned a 13-millimetre wound and goes on to describe lacerated, pulmonary tissue. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The thoracic cavity has to be opened up, and only then can one describe all the changes within the thoracic cavity, including the change of the kind described here, such as compression and laceration of the pulmonary tissue. This is not appropriate, not even with a larger, much larger wound can you do with only such a basic description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In item 11 of Exhibit P70, can we see at all from this description whether the thoracic cavity was opened up?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: From what I see, the thoracic cavity had not been opened up at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event that the thoracic cavity had been opened up, would that have to be indicated in the record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Certainly. All the elements and the contents of the thoracic cavity which are many, and it would take me a long time to tell you all the things we can find in the thoracic cavity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the usher's assistance, I would like to show the witness Exhibit P74.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: Interpreters also need these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, Prosecution Exhibit P74 constitutes an excerpt from the book of death certificates, or rather, register of deaths in the area of Skocko Tonci.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please look at the first rubric indicating the day, month, and hour of death which has to be recorded according to the form. We see the 6th of December 1991, 0910 hours. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. In Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Was it possible to determine based on such work of the pathologist that we saw in the previous exhibit, P70, was it possible to determine such an exact time of death for the indicated person?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Not even with many more medical parameters is it possible to determine the minute of death unless the person died while being connected to some sort of life-supporting equipment or ECG. It is very difficult to speak of the minute of death. It is even difficult to determine the hour, let alone the minute. And in this case, it was absolutely impossible to determine the exact time of death based on the postmortem that had been presented to me for Tonci Skocko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you, with reference to the entire record of external examination of bodies, marked as P70, and I'm now interested in the examination of all the bodies, all the 19 of them, and the descriptions entered for them as noted in the record, was it possible to determine the exact time of death?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: On the basis of what was medically established, no. The examination was completely inadequate; descriptions were completely inadequate. And the pathologist based on what was written and the parameters included was absolutely unable to determine the time of death. Even, if I may add, that is what a postmortem is for. An external examination is very important, but it is the postmortem that establishes the content of urine, the contents of the stomach, type of contents, and all these elements are very important for the pathologist to determine the time of death. Based on the description that we saw, I shall repeat in very modest terms, very mild terms, it was impossible to determine the time of death.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you certainly noticed in the record of external examination of dead bodies marked as P70 under item 5 and under item 9 two dead bodies, two male dead bodies were described, unidentified bodies. Would you tell me from the viewpoint of your profession and in view of your regulations, and bearing in mind the descriptions given under 5 and 9, is it possible to determine the identity of these persons subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: In my judgement, it is not possible. A sample of these bodies would have to be left aside, and that would have been recorded. But first of all, all the established changes had to be described, all the characteristics of the corpses, plus a number of identifying elements in order to leave room for subsequent work to identify the body or to have the bodies identified by relatives or other interested parties. Or maybe a part of the body should have been preserved in order to make a DNA analysis later. But how can you make a DNA analysis if a postmortem does not provide basic information to narrow down the possibilities? In this case, I believe the possibility of identifying the bodies subsequently has been ruled out due to subsequent changes, the disintegration of certain tissues, and the decay, the general decay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you look at the record of external examination of dead bodies marked as Exhibit P70, it says that the pathologist had begun his work at 0915 hours. And at the end of the record, it is indicated that the work was completed at 1300 hours. My question is: Would three hours and 45 minutes be sufficient time to precisely identify and describe changes on 19 bodies even if it had only been an external examination requiring the description of external findings only?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: If the work is done properly in medical terms, then the pathologist accompanied by an assistant and having a Dictaphone or a secretary able to type simultaneously, which is another possibility, it would be possible to conduct a postmortem within 20 minutes if there are no wounds. That is an absolute minimum. I don't know anybody who would be able to complete a postmortem on a body without any wounds in a shorter time. From what I see from these records, most of the bodies were dressed. The clothes had to be removed, described. The contents of the clothes described. Deformities, if any, on the clothes would also have to be described. The body would then have to be washed and establish all the changes in detail. This cannot be done if you do your work properly using only 40 minutes per body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibits P72 and P71.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is it visible from this whether there was any clothing on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, both bodies were dressed. The clothing was partly removed, partly torn, possibly because urgent assistance needed to be administered at some point. But there are remaining clothes on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During an external examination of a dead body, in this specific case, these 19 bodies, is it necessary to also remove clothing from the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Certainly. Absolutely. And it has to be described in detail as well as the changes on the clothing and anything found in or on the clothing, at least in the medical school that I follow, in order to be able to record it. Among other things, because changes on the clothing may indicate the type of object used to inflict death, so the clothing has to be removed, and all the details have to be described. If it is technically possible, colour photographs have to be taken as well if so envisaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, within the 20-minute minimum that you indicated as required for an external examination of a body without any wounds involved under ideal circumstances, would those 20 minutes also cover this procedure; namely, the removal of clothing from the body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, no. 20 minutes is the time that I thought would be required by an experienced pathologist accompanied by an assistant to describe the minimum 20 parameters that I mentioned because the content and size of cavities have to be described, measured. All this has to be done. And if there are any deformities on the clothing on top of that, at least 40 minutes would be required. And even that is only my estimate of the time I would require after having performed 1.500 postmortems in cases of violent death, as I submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, Doctor, your curriculum vitae is much more voluminous than the version I presented to the Court. And we sort of skipped through that part in my introductory examination.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: If I may conclude about this required time, if you do the work properly, it is absolutely impossible to examine 19 bodies in three hours, 45 minutes, if the pathologist is working according to the professional regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown the following documents: P56, P57, and P59.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please look at Prosecution Exhibit P57. This is a release form from the medical centre in Dubrovnik dated the 12th of December 1991. The name is Mato Valjalo.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: All right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at this and tell us whether the diagnosis that is presented here in the Latin language corresponds to the description of injuries established during the examination which was described in the upper part above the diagnosis in this medical document. Are there several pieces of shrapnel in the body? That is what I'm specifically interested in.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: As for this description, first of all, in the mother tongue, it was established that the patient had received explosive wounds in the region of the neck and in the region of the right thigh. In the diagnosis in the Latin language, it says that he received explosive wounds in the area of the neck, in the area of the thigh, but what is mentioned is that he was also wounded in the right shoulder blade area, and there is no reference to that in what it says in the mother tongue previously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have a single document. Could we please have something placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the diagnosis is not in keeping with the description of injuries established beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. The difference is that in Latin, it says that injuries were sustained in the right shoulder blade area, which was not noted in the previous description. I can show you that if need be. This is what it says here, "explosive wounds in the area of the neck and in the area of the right thigh." Later on, in the diagnosis in Latin, there is additional information, reg scapular dex, that's what it says. So that includes the right shoulder blade area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Doctor, in these findings, is there any mention of shrapnel in the body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I do not see shrapnel mentioned here at all. I just see a description of explosive wound. I do not see any mention of shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please look at P56 now. This is a letter of discharge in the name of Mato Valjalo. The document was issued by the clinical centre of Rijeka. The date is the 9th of January 1992. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, I've already placed it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this document, in the hospital in Rijeka, a metal foreign object, 3 by 1 centimetre, was taken out Mato Valjalo's body. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the medical documents that I studied, Mato Valjalo, after having been wounded in -- or rather, after having stayed at the Dubrovnik medical centre from the 6th until the 12th of December 1991 was transferred to the surgery ward of the clinical hospital centre in Rijeka, and he was treated there in the following interval: From the 16th of December until -- that is to say, the 16th of December 1991 until the 9th of January 1992. On the ninth day after he was admitted at the surgery ward in Rijeka, he was operated on. And surgery was performed then in order to remove this foreign metal body from the area of his neck. It was described as shrapnel, the dimensions being 3 by 1 centimetres. After having stayed further on at that institute, he was discharged from that hospital and sent for rehabilitation in Opatija. That is what is mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, it says that Mato Valjalo's neck was x-rayed, and that a foreign metal object was seen there, the dimensions being 3 by 1 centimetres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to these findings, in the x-ray of Mato Valjalo, was only this one piece of shrapnel seen, or rather, was it established that there was only this one metal foreign body of these dimensions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Only one piece of shrapnel was described. That particular one, 3 by 1 centimetres. There is no mention of any other shrapnel or are any other dimensions given. Only that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, was this confirmed in the diagnosis in Latin which is mentioned at the very beginning of this document? There is a diagnosis in the Latin language.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. Only one piece of shrapnel is mentioned in the Latin language as well. It is in the singular. Just a moment, please. Could I just say something else. All right, that's what I think -- corpus -- I mean -- now I'm trying to think back and remember the Latin I learned during my university studies, the second declension and things like that. But what is noticeable from this document is there is reference to one single piece of shrapnel only. As far as I know, if it's in the plural, it should say corpori alienii, with a double "i". In the second word, it does say "alieni," but if it is in the plural, there needs to be a double "i" at the end, so this is wrong anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please look further on in the same document, P56, or rather the next document within this exhibit is a letter of discharge from the specialised hospital for rehabilitation, Thalassotherapia in Opatija, dated the 26th of February 1992, again, in the name of Mato Valjalo. Do you have this document before you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please, in this document from the hospital in Opatija, does it say that several foreign objects were removed from Mato Valjalo's body in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: After having stayed at the hospital at Rijeka and after this one foreign body, 3 by 1 centimetres, was removed from his body, according to this medical documentation, Mato Valjalo went for rehabilitation in Opatija. Further on, it says that at the KBC in Rijeka, several foreign metal objects were removed from his body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Doctor, these findings from Opatija, do they collide with the findings from Rijeka that you looked at beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course they collide. In my opinion they collide, because any surgeon would be duty-bound to say what kind of operation he carried out. So he would have to refer to other foreign bodies that he had extracted. So I believe that the surgeon would have noted the removal of other foreign objects as well. There is no reference to that whatsoever in this Rijeka documentation.
