utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please look at P56 again, but the third document, namely the letter of discharge in the name of Mato Valjalo issued by the hospital in Zagreb where Mato Valjalo stayed from the 13th until the 25th of March 1994. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Sir, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to the following: Is there any difference in the description of the wounds established in this letter of discharge in relation to the first medical findings from Dubrovnik dated the 12th of December 1991? That is the first letter of discharge from December 1991. Could you please compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The next medical document in the name of Mato Valjalo is the medical document from the general hospital in Zagreb from the department of internal medicine where Mato Valjalo was treated between the 13th and 25th of March 1994. In that institution, he was examined in detail, and it says towards the end, there are actually diagnoses in the Latin language. And one of them says that the situation after -- says that the situation after the explosive wound in the neck area, or rather, the status after that, because according to these medical documents this wound was sustained in 1991. So it was only an explosive wound in the neck area. And it differs from the first medical document that refers to wounds in the right thigh area and the right shoulder blade area. This medical document is similar to the Rijeka medical document. The one from Zagreb and the one from Rijeka refer to a wound in the neck area only, just one wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please look at Prosecution Exhibit P59 now.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Okay, I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit P59. Doctor, Exhibit P59 is not in front of you as far as I can see. That is supposed to be a document from the medical centre in Dubrovnik in the name of Mato Valjalo dated the 13th of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: This is one of the documents that remain behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there has been some confusion. This medical document probably underwent a permutation during its numbering. Can we proceed now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us now what kind of document this is within P59.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: This is a piece of paper. This is only part of the history of illness. And also, there is part of the personal file that comes from the medical centre in Dubrovnik. This document shows that Mato Valjalo, it says, was wounded on the 6th of December 1991 in the neck area, in the chest area, and in the leg area with remaining shrapnel in the right leg, in the lungs, and in the neck. That is what this document states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question in relation to P59 dated the 13th of March 1995 stating that Mato Valjalo still has foreign objects in his body; the organ indicated is the lungs. Now, my question is, have we seen a single document so far to do with Mato Valjalo that contained any reference whatsoever to lungs or any foreign object in the lungs of Mato Valjalo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No. It was the first time at the end of this document that I found there were any foreign bodies in the lung tissue. Otherwise, the patient was very carefully examined, that's what I can say, after looking at his medical files in the department of internal medicine in Zagreb. And his thoracic cavity was -- his chest was x-rayed. I think that is a sufficiently reliable method to ascertain if there are any foreign objects in the lung tissue. So I can't really understand how these foreign objects in the lung tissue have turned up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, an examination of the chest and an x-ray of the chest were carried out one year earlier in Zagreb. That was in 1994. Mato Valjalo was thoroughly examined. Do you think that pieces of shrapnel in the lungs would have been discovered during that examination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. An x-ray is usually accurate enough to indicate any pieces of shrapnel in the lungs. But there's no reference to this in the medical files of the department for internal medicine in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In P59, there is a sentence which reads: "Still contains foreign objects, shrapnel," and then after the lungs, it talks about the neck, "shrapnel in the neck." Is this something new in relation to shrapnel in the neck that was mentioned in P56, in the letter of discharge from the clinical medical centre in Rijeka dated the 9th of January 1992 which says that one foreign metal object was found in the neck after an x-ray, the dimensions being 3 by 1 centimetres, and that this was surgically removed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, there's an important difference there, in the Rijeka institution, Rijeka surgery, according to the medical files, one piece of shrapnel was removed. That is by no means small, the dimensions being 3 by 1 centimetres in the right-hand side of the neck, which is a very delicate spot, of course. But there is no other reference to pieces of shrapnel being there, whereas now we have reference to further pieces of shrapnel in the neck but there's no trace of this in the Rijeka medical files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to run this past you again. That document, P56, in relation to the letter of discharge from the Zagreb general hospital in the name of Mato Valjalo dated 1994, was a thorough examination of Mato Valjalo carried out, especially in relation to his chest and lungs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, that's a different one. Yes. This is the most comprehensive medical file that I have seen here so far, the one from Zagreb, the most detailed one. There is reference there to an examination of the chest. That's item 4 in this document. And there was nothing to lead me to believe that while the patient was in hospital in Zagreb, any pieces of shrapnel were found or discovered in the lung tissue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Doctor, about patient Mato Valjalo, let me ask you the following: Are there, in fact, two identical findings to be found anywhere in terms of how they describe any shrapnel in his body or the injuries sustained by Mato Valjalo? If you look at all these different medical files from Rijeka, Zagreb, Dubrovnik, and Opatija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: None of the diagnoses given in Latin are consistent. The description of shrapnel in Mato Valjalo's body is not consistent either. The Zagreb files and the Rijeka files are two files that are quite similar, but there are, in fact, no identical files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that an x-ray is a method which is accurate enough to ascertain the presence in the body of a foreign body, a foreign metal body such as a piece of shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, based on the medical files that you have looked at in relation to Ivo Vlasica, can one ascertain which wound Ivo Vlasica -- which of Ivo Vlasica's legs were actually wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It wasn't possible for me to ascertain which of his legs actually sustained the wounds. And that is what I wrote in my expert opinion. Reference here is to a wound to the left leg. These are the files of the general hospital in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P84, Exhibit P84. It's an OTP exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you the findings, and then we can pick up from there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I have some of those with me, and that is what I based my opinion on. But if you say so ... I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, which document do you have in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What I have in front of me now, what I'm looking at is a document from the general hospital from Dubrovnik, the surgery ward, dated the 18th of February 1994. And the name is Ivo Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you read this document, if you look at the description that it contains in relation to the examination of Ivo Vlasica, do you think that the wounds are sufficiently described in this finding from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, they are not sufficiently described. And I must say I'm speaking about my experience with doctors from the former Yugoslavia, people I'm often in touch with, and it's still the same. Doctors often find it very difficult to describe all the parameters of the wound, and according to the rules at least six of those must be given, its exact location, the size, or rather the diameter, the edges and sides with entry and exit wounds, and the channel that the wound has created. You must also describe the surrounding area, normally. In this document, the only description we find is a reference to a tangential entry and exit wound to the left upper leg, therefore this is the kind of body we are looking at, and the location is given, that is between the upper third and middle third. And there is also reference to profuse bleeding. We can't say this is an adequate description. It is, in fact, inadequate, because the size of the wound is not given. The only thing that is actually given here is the location of the wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you look at these findings and the description of the wound contained therein, can you notice a difference in terms of the mechanism by which the wound was caused? Could you say, based on this description, whether the wound was caused by shrapnel or by a missile that was fired from a hand-held weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Based on the description that was provided by the pathologist, it's impossible to ascertain which kind of wound we are looking at. No way. You have to enumerate and describe the parameters that I've referred to in order to be able later to define what the tool was that had caused the injury.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this specific finding, do we find any description at all about how this tangential entry and exit wound to the left upper leg came about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No such thing, no. The only description we find is tangential entry and exit wound, its location, profuse bleeding, but we can't tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which wound it is that is bleeding profusely, whether it's the entry wound or the exit wound. So all we have here is that one of the wounds is bleeding. Therefore, it's insufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, in your professional career, have you ever dealt with wounds caused by shrapnel or wounds caused by a missile fired from a hand-held weapon, specifically wounds caused by a bullet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I wish to point out that where I live, unfortunately, I've had plenty of opportunities to work with that sort of wound, both caused by shrapnel and by a missile, which does not exactly make me a happy man. So the answer so your question is: Yes, I've had many occasions to deal with those types of wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any difference and what is the difference between a wound that is caused by shrapnel and a wound that is caused by a missile from a hand-held weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: In the case of shrapnel, the wounds are usually big and gaping, usually there's one dominant wound with profuse bleeding. Inside the wound and at the bottom of the wound, you have torn and bleeding soft tissue at the extremities and around the edges of the wound usually you have pieces of broken bone. So this would be a rough description. In the case of missiles, the sort used by hand-held weapons such as pistols or revolvers, you usually have tangential entry and exit wounds with varying diameters. Mostly, in our area, when the wounds stem from a pistol or revolver, the diameter would be around 8 millimetres with less bleeding. This would be a brief description more or less. I could give you plenty more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this finding, do we have a description of the wound whether it was caused by a hand-held missile or by shrapnel? Do we find a description such as you have just said should be there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: There is no such description. There should be a description, or it should be photographed by the pathologists, and this should be attached to the medical files. There should be some sort of a rough description, at least. The diameter, the size, the edges. If there's no time to do that, you usually take colour photographs, and these then form part of the medical files, none of which we find here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the description in this document, P84, the entry indicates a tangential entry and exit wound to the left upper leg. The diagnosis in Latin reads: "Vulnus explossivum femoris sin." What I want to know is: When we have an entry and exit wound, in the Latin language, is there a specific diagnosis to describe that sort of wound?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The main diagnosis, a true medical diagnosis would be vulnus sclopetarium femoris in this case, since you must locate the wound. The part of the subspecies of the vulnus sclopetarium would be an explosive wound. Some doctors who have not been sufficiently trained use the expression vulnus trans sclopetarium, and this prefix "trans" should denote an exit and entry wound, but that's erroneous. Therefore, if you find the description vulnus sclopetarium, that's okay. Of course, later on, you must add a clarification. This is an exit and entry wound, so you describe in other words. But all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness annexes A, B, C, and D that have been admitted into evidence by decision of the Trial Chamber of the 26th of May 2004. These exhibits have not been numbered, Your Honours, at least the numbers are not mentioned in the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 26th of May. And let me remind everybody, these documents refer to Ivo Vlasica presented by the Prosecution at the end of their case. And apart from oral arguments, we have presented our written submissions thereon after which the Trial Chamber decided that these documents be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will now have an exhibit number, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, they actually do, P86.1, P86.2, and P86.3. I think the Registrar marked them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. P86.1, .2, and .3 are documents that were introduced during examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, and they were marked for identification, whereas these are different documents presented by the Prosecution subsequently after the end of their case in May. One is the hospital protocol for Ivo Vlasica, case history, plus another two medical documents which, as you remember, we argued in oral and in writing. And by decision of the Trial Chamber of the 26th of May 2004, these two documents were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, they were the subject of our decision. And the decision required that a number be allocated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I stand corrected. If those are the documents, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am told that together they are Exhibit P211, 2-1-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English. Everything is in English, at least this part. There is a statement by Dr. Jaksa Segedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not need the statement by Dr. Jaksa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a protocol from a hospital in front of you? It contains a group of documents in B/C/S. Please look at this one. It is an excerpt from a medical protocol. And under number 972, Ivo Vlasica is mentioned. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this diagnosis in Latin. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course I can. Literally translated, it means gunshot wound to the thigh, explosive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it an entry and exit wound or just the gunshot wound?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course, we cannot see from this document what it is. It says only that it is a wound inflicted by a firearm. There are actually three types, entry wounds, entry and exit wounds, and grazing wounds which also fall within the category of sclopetaria wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That is under A. Look at the next document under B, which should be the case history of Ivo Vlasica. Did you find that? The date is 6th of December 1991 as date of admission; date of discharge is the 21st of December 1991. What do these X1, E1, mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could we have this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the diagnosis means. I don't know about these abbreviations and acronyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the Latin diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The same as in the previous case. Gunshot wound. I can only surmise. I see a dot above the I. It is an explosive gunshot wound to the left thigh. That's what's written in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the next page. Case history as given by the patient and finding. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see in handwriting "wounded on the 6th of December 1991 by shrapnel before the shop where he works, Dubrovkinja, the name of the shop. Immediately transferred to the medical centre." If I see -- if I read this well, it says "never undergone surgery before."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I cannot translate the second word, but I agree with you that it should mean no previous surgical history. Those are the third, fourth, and fifth words. I don't know what the second word could be. Maybe healthy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look below in the typed part of the text. It says "Vlasica, it was established on the basis of clinical findings that this was a tangential projectile wound of the left upper leg, more laterally on the border of the upper and middle third, with profuse bleeding from the wound." Would that correspond to this first document, P84, from the 18th of February 1994 since therapy and drainage are mentioned? That was the first document, if you remember, relating to Ivo Vlasica.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have a look at it now. This is the same description as in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you see that this is a case history, the case history for Ivo Vlasica, this document P211, whereas P84 is a copy issued to Ivo Vlasica on the 18th of February 1994, would such a copy or transcript be issued on the basis of a case history?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Based on the case history, a certain document can be issued by way of certificate. You don't have to give the patient the entire case history upon request. You can issue for any sort of purpose, such as for purposes of the court, a part of the documentation available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know something about the question of whether it was the left or right leg. In the case history for Ivo Vlasica, P211, and in the transcript of findings on his injury, P84, do these two coincide as to the injury being to the left leg?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Both say that Ivo Vlasica was wounded in the left thigh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at P211, Doctor, item C, which is the report of the specialist dated 6th December 1991. Yes, that document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read for us what it says.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I'm speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to take care for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: This specialist, surgeon Stjepan Bogdanovic, wrote that Ivo Vlasica was wounded in the right leg, femoris dex, that is that it was an explosive wound to the right thigh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same as the finding of the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, this finding dates to the 6th December, Dr. Stjepan Bogdanovic, senior surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you compare it to the case history and the transcript or the copy from P211, the case history and the excerpt marked P84 dated 18th February 1994, would you say that these two speak of two different extremities, two different legs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Dr. Bogdanovic speaks of the right leg, that is, the surgeon, whereas the case history and the first document, which is a copy or an excerpt, speaks of the left leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, in the same document, P211, marked as D, look at annex D or item D.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Very well. If you mean the x-ray report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. X-ray report and opinion dated 6th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. In the name of Ivo Vlasica, performed by J. Dragicevic or something like that. It's different to see the initial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, what is said in the handwritten part below the words "x-ray report and opinion"? What was done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: This was again written in hand. I'll try to read it. "The image of the right upper leg" -- well, I cannot read this. "Neither foreign bodies" -- it's hard to read. If I can be free to guess, this says it doesn't show either fractures or foreign bodies. The image of the right upper leg does not show any fractures or foreign bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same has been translated into English. "Either fractures or foreign bodies." What does this mean now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: This means that the x-ray did not confirm anything. Either the gunshot wound or any other injury to the right leg. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this x-ray report does not confirm the previous reports we have seen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Only the right leg is described in this x-ray report. But it says that there is nothing in the right leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question for you, Doctor -- in fact, I withdraw this question. I'll rephrase it. In your experience and in your practice and according to the rules of your profession, how does a doctor examine a patient? By which methods?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I think I understand your question. The description of injuries is always performed looking at the front of the patient with arms hanging freely alongside the body, if the patient is able to assume that position which is called physiological position. This is how changes are identified looking at a patient in that position. That's the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm facing you, Doctor, and I am wearing a bandage or an injury to my right arm, what will you write in your report? Which of my arms is injured?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Your right arm, of course. But you wouldn't have to stand like this. You would have to let your arms hang freely alongside your body. Of course, the position of your right arm does not change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, have you ever heard or seen in your practice of a doctor facing the patient while examining him or her with a patient having an injury to their right arm, and the doctor writing of an injury to the left arm or leg simply because from the doctor's side it looks as left?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Something would have to be very wrong with that doctor. I've never heard of anything of the kind. It is simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... We will adjourn now for a short lunch break, resuming at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is it? Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. Do -- is it Dr. Soc? Can I just make -- to sure I've got your name pronounced correctly, is it Soc?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, Soc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told Mr. Rodic about your experience over the years and having performed thousands of autopsies. When did you perform your first autopsy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: My first autopsy was while I was doing my specialist course. I don't know whether it was exactly on the first day, but I started my specialist course in May 1990 in Belgrade. And, of course, in the presence of my mentors, I did my first autopsy during the first month of my work, so it must be in June. So the first autopsy I did was on a body of a person who had hanged himself. It was a suicide. And I did it with a mentor who was a Belgrade professor, Professor Obradovic, and that was probably in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All I want to do is to ask you -- a very, very simple question was when. I was only after the date. I know you want to tell us more, but please. Otherwise, we'll be here for a lot longer. Thank you. I think you said that you were working in Podgorica from 1992 on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working in Belgrade between 1990 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. I was doing my specialist course. I was doing my residency, so that went on for two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that at a university in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you doing autopsies in the course of your studying for your specialisation over those two years in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working at a teaching hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The exact name is the Institute for Forensic Medicine of the School of Medicine of the University of Belgrade. That is the exact name of that institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- is it the best facility for learning the art of forensic pathology and autopsies in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: May I give my own free opinion? I believe the answer would be yes. And even beyond that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us it is a well-equipped, modern, functioning facility? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion about that institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was -- it was also well equipped, modern, and functioning when you were working there in 1990 to 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, that is my opinion, because I haven't got much experience. After Podgorica, I went there to school. I was admitted. And the only thing I could do was to make comparisons within the former Yugoslavia, and that is the oldest school of its kind. It is now celebrating its 81st anniversary, this school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The institution at which you work in Podgorica, is that the premier medical facility in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The clinical centre where I work now is supposed to be the best institution of its kind in my republic. That is its reputation. It is the only clinical centre, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also describe it as well equipped, modern, and functioning, and has been since you have been there since 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I could give a critical opinion of my own institution where I work now rather than the institute in Belgrade in terms of equipment and the working conditions because I believe that it is not the best possible equipment by any means. I can just tell you that I don't have a mobile x-ray machine, that I cannot do DNA analysis. But that institution in 1999 was physically reconstructed -- actually, we worked in an institution that covered 600 square metres in physical terms. And that is where the department of pathology now is, and for histology and anatomy. And now we have about 2.000 square metres all together. However, that is not nearly enough at the level of western Europe. It's not really at that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Dubrovnik hospital in November or December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: The last time I was in Croatia in general was on the 14th of February 1991 when I passed my oral masters examination at the school of medicine at the University of Zagreb in the presence of my professors there, again, at the institute of forensic medicine. I haven't been in Zagreb since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are unaware of the circumstances prevailing at Dubrovnik hospital in November and December 1991. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you have performed -- withdraw that. In the course of performing autopsies, have you ever done so without the benefit of electricity or running water?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a problem with my minister, too, because there was a shortage of water in 1999. While I was doing three autopsies in Bar, when I refused to perform further autopsies after the first autopsy because I believe that water is a minimum requirement. As for electricity, if there is daylight, an autopsy can be completed because bones can be opened manually, the skull, the rib cage, et cetera. But I think that in all forensic medicine manuals, it says that water is a minimum requirement. But yes, I did work even without water. I just remembered now - I'm sorry - I also worked at the border of the Pljevlja municipality in the north of Montenegro when there were conflicts with the Muslims, and I did autopsies in the field without either water or electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're saying that running water is a minimum requirement to do a proper, full autopsy according to forensic medical texts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I believe, that there has to be water, at least in bottles or in other containers. I think that an autopsy should not even be started if there is no water. It doesn't have to be running water; it can be water from a bottle, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the largest number of autopsies that you have performed in a day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, so far in my life, I have carried out a maximum of five entire autopsies within 24 hours; and within 48 hours, I carried out external examinations of 18 bodies of persons who were victims of traffic accidents. And I conducted this with three assistants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the one in which you carried out the examination of 18 bodies, was that after a traumatic event, like a bus smash? What I'm asking you, what was the reason for there being 18 bodies there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They weren't entire autopsies. These were 18 external examinations like the ones conducted here. I had to carry out these 18 external examinations because those were the orders received from the investigating judge who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the event. What precipitated it? Was it a bus crash or something like that? Were 18 bodies brought in because there had been a road accident?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right. There was a road accident near Titograd in the canyon of Platr [phoen]. A bus fell into the canyon of the Moraca River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course in ideal circumstances, the best that you could probably perform in a day would be between two and three; that's autopsies, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I think that for an individual, for one doctor, that is a lot. That is a major psychological effort. I think that that is very much for one day. Analysing the data I have so far, if a pathologist does one autopsy per day, even that is a great burden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of autopsies or examinations a pathologist may perform in a day depends on a lot of circumstances such as the facilities available, the staff available, and the number of bodies, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in an emergency situation such as the bus crash or a bomb blast or a fire or in war, it would be fair to say that the standards of autopsy or examination may diminish according to the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No. Standards cannot be changed. The rules have to be the same regardless of danger to the pathologist's life, and everything has to be done in proper order; otherwise, it's all wrong. Of course, many examinations or autopsies within a short span of time is a major effort, an enormous effort on the part of the pathologist. But the professional standards may not be infringed upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is I'm asking you to accept that -- withdraw that. When you spoke about the rules of forensic medicine and they must be complied with, which you did when Mr. Rodic questioned you, I take it you were referring to the methodology employed rather than the law which was in force in the Republic of Croatia as on the 7th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the law was in 1991 on that day in Croatia, in 1991. I see that this was done on the basis of the order issued by the investigating judge, as we do. But I pointed out that the examinations were not done properly, regardless of on whose orders they were done. I still abide by what I said, that these corpses were not examined properly and professionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I again ask you if possible to please confine your answer. I was asking you about the methodology or the law, which is one or the other. A moment ago you said "standards cannot be changed. The rules have to be the same regardless of the danger." Now, even accepting that standards, that is, the standard itself cannot be changed, the practical circumstances change from hospital to hospital and situation to situation, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I cannot give a yes or no answer. Different hospitals have different working conditions. But the actual medical work has to be done strictly in compliance with the rules of the science of medicine. But, of course, working conditions vary from one medical institution to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Conditions, of course, are different in war and peacetime, and the possibilities of complying with standards are different in war and peace, aren't they? What I'm saying is what is possible in peace, in ideal circumstances, may not be possible in a hospital in a war zone?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Certainly when circumstances change, the mental setup of a pathologist also changes. But he must do his work according to the rules. You told me not to go into any details, but what I would like to point out is that I myself worked under NATO bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of how many pathologists, forensic pathologists there were at Dubrovnik hospital in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I believe in the Dubrovnik area, there is not a single specialised pathologist. Back in 1991, not a single person, not a single expert who had actually taken and completed any specialised courses in forensic medicine. I believe there was only one expert in clinical pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dr. Ciganovic who was the forensic pathologist in Dubrovnik was also the chief pathologist at the hospital; that is, he was doing two jobs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: There is no doubt in my mind that he perhaps may be a clinical pathologist, but I do not believe that he completed any courses in forensic pathology. That is, at least, my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion is based upon your reading of the examination or autopsy report. Is that all it's based on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: There's another bit of information, too. I know a colleague who works back in Montenegro, and I know that prior to 1991, prior to the war, he would often go and work in the Dubrovnik area from Montenegro, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you to accept is that in a situation in a war in which 19 bodies are brought in on the same day with a description of them all having been killed the day before, and there's only one person who can deal with it, one couldn't possibly expect the same standards that you would apply in peacetime to be applied to the work that is done, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I understand the stress levels that were involved in my colleagues' work under those conditions that you have referred to. The one thing I cannot accept is that someone conducts such deficient examinations of the bodies, such incomplete examinations, although I do accept that the circumstances must have been very difficult. It must have been very difficult to work under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you there was no water, according to the evidence, no electricity, the doctor believed he was in a lull in the shelling, and there may be more bodies coming in, would you accept that in those circumstances the standards for performing the autopsies or examinations have to be lessened according to these particular emergency circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I can't accept that, I'm afraid. It would be the same if you were asking me if on account of war conditions, a surgeon should perform an operation in a way that is contrary to the rules of the medical science. The only way he's allowed to proceed is according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, rules, you told us a little bit earlier, or according to your own examination of the bodies in the bus crash, were external examinations. It's clear from Dr. Ciganovic's report that he did a number of external examinations just as you would have done, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I carried out external examinations because I had been ordered by the investigating judge to do so. But I also insisted that an autopsy be performed on the driver. This request was not complied with, though. All the findings, and this should be easy enough to verify, were done according to my instructions in all the specific cases, with all the descriptions that I provided. These files are kept in Podgorica, and this should be easy to check. I included all the 20 parameters. I described the wounds. I identified the bodies, which is difficult work in view of the presence of the parents of those deceased. But I stood up to defend the principles that I spoke about before this Honourable Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Autopsy or examination is only one way of determining a cause of death, isn't it? There are other ways, in combination, of determining a cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that is one way. There are clinical methods, too, to establish a diagnosis prior to an autopsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience under war and under NATO bombing and of experiences in the former Yugoslavia tells you that people can be killed from shelling, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A shell exploding 40 to 50 metres away from a person, exploding with fragments of shrapnel flying about, fragments could enter a person and kill them, or cause an injury leading to their death?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A shell exploding closer -- I withdraw that. And the -- you may expect to see an explosive wound from flying shrapnel. I say "may."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It may be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a shell exploding closer to a person could cause blast injuries and kill them instantly, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That may be an another circumstance involved that's beyond doubt. Lives can be lost when a person is hit by shrapnel from as far away as 40 metres from where the person is actually standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your experience of wartime has told you or taught you that when there is a sustained shelling of an urban environment, you may expect to see casualties bearing the same sorts of injuries, either dead or alive, on the same day, from the shelling, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's quite possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that Dubrovnik, the Old Town and the Dubrovnik area, was under shelling on the 6th of December 1991, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: All I know about this I know from the public media. As a citizen of my country, I know about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you -- you will accept for the purposes of these questions that there were shells landing in the Old Town and the surrounding area over a period of hours on the 6th of December 1991, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, I'm a doctor. If that is a fact, I accept it. I vehemently opposed any war in my own country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at Dr. Ciganovic's report of his examinations, you'll see that all of the injuries there are consistent with injury from shelling, aren't they? Shell fire or gunfire or war, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, this colleague of mine who did that wrote down that those were explosive wounds, but he did not describe the wounds. He proceeded immediately to describe them as explosive wounds, and the rule of our science is that the wounds must first be described so that any further experts who may be examining the files may see what the wounds are about, whereas here they are immediately identified as blast injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just taking the identification and the description of shelling over hours before, the description of blast injuries or explosive injuries, that combined with the fact that there are 19 people being brought in on the same day can lead you to conclude that it's consistent with these people having been the victims of shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm a doctor. I'm telling you about what the medical files say. I never said those people weren't dead, nor did I state that there had been no explosions as a result of which they were killed. Never crossed my mind to say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the circumstances described in examination, the same -- more or less the same cause of death is diagnosed. There has been shelling the day before, and there's a number of -- 19 people brought in in a fairly small area on the same day. That makes it likely that those people all share the same cause of death, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Quite probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with or do you know exactly what Dr. Ciganovic did in relation to his examination of Pavo Urban? That's body number 15. Or is your only information what is contained in that report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: My information is based on the medical files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your curriculum vitae says that you speak English. Have you been provided with a copy of the transcript of his evidence as to what he said in this Tribunal about how he performed the autopsies or the examinations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any transcripts. I do speak English. Well, of course, I always require assistance because I don't get to speak English very often, and it's not particularly fluent. But I can't say I've seen that particular portion of the transcript, or what Dr. Ciganovic stated, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at least not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He described circumstances in which he performed what he called a partial autopsy, which he did in the prevailing circumstances. Are you aware that that's what he did?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: What I'm going by is what I have in the medical files. I know about nothing else that was or was not done. The only thing I based my opinion on, if you allow, is on these medical files that were forwarded to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- withdraw that. Dr. Ciganovic told the Trial Chamber that this is -- this is what he did, this is how he performed it. In the circumstances at Dubrovnik hospital without water, electricity -- running water, electricity, and during what he said was a lull in the shelling with 19 bodies there, where necessary he performed a partial autopsy which was, quote -- he would do an external examination, examine the clothes, the skin, and any other external marks of injury, and proceed to examine the depth of the injury in order to determine the channel and the depth of the wound, the direction of the channel, the intensity of the damage sustained by the internal organs, and also, to reach, if I could, the object that caused the injury, which more often than not was lodged inside the victim's body. This entailed partially opening parts of the body, specific parts of the body where the injury occurred so that I could get inside by using my instruments and have a look. Unquote. That's at page 2741. You've just told us you were aware that that was what he did to help him establish the cause of death. What I'm suggesting is that in the circumstances prevailing, the shelling, the lack of water, electricity, the number of bodies, he being the only person, would you go so far as to say that was probably the best that he could do in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, what you're putting to me now is much different from what I found in the medical files. There's more description. I'm not sure if anyone had looked at the clothes, but I've seen no description of the clothing. If someone had actually succeeded in removing the clothes and going through them, this is something I have never come across in these files. I cannot doubt that this was done, but it's simply not in the files that I have seen. That's all I'm saying. There are several activities here that were described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate it's not in the files. That's the evidence Dr. Ciganovic gave in this Trial Chamber. What I'm asking you about is your opinion. Would you accept that in all of those circumstances, the 19 bodies, the only person available, the lack of facilities, that this was the best he could do in those extreme circumstances? And he only did so when he felt that he needed to do so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to challenge that, the sequence of actions under those circumstances, the external examination under duress in circumstances that were difficult. And that's how the work was done. I can't challenge that. But I don't see anything recorded in the files. It's difficult to speak about things that I don't see in the files. I do accept that that was the only thing he could do, and especially considering that he had been ordered to carry out external examinations and not autopsies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you haven't read Dr. Ciganovic's evidence. Are we to take it you also haven't read the evidence in relation to the death of Tonci Skocko and the witness who described what happened to him before he was brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only thing I've looked at are the medical files. I have nothing else except for the medical files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence before the Tribunal is of this 18-year-old young man walking out into the street during the shelling on the morning at about 9.00 or so, the 6th of December, and a shell exploding close by in a narrow -- one of those narrow streets in Dubrovnik, and him walking back into the shop and collapsing with blood on his chest and being taken unconscious to hospital and being dead on arrival, and the autopsy being performed -- the partial autopsy being performed the next day. In these circumstances, you've got two pieces of evidence as to the cause of death. One is the eyewitness evidence of the shell, him being struck, being taken unconscious to hospital; and the second one is a partial autopsy revealing an explosive injury. You understand that scenario?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I'm only waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, that is, the partial autopsy and the results in the medical files, and the eyewitness description of what happened to the boy the day before, you as a doctor could safely conclude, couldn't you, that shelling was the cause of this person's death?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can be literal, shelling cannot be the cause of death. Shelling could have caused the injury by shrapnel whereas causes of death are embolus, sepsis, bleeding out, et cetera. Shelling can be a mechanism of injury which in its turn leads to the cause of death, as I said many times here in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stand completely corrected by the way you have described it. I meant it in a more general, lay sort of term, that shelling in those circumstances was the thing that caused the injury which led to the blood loss which killed this young man.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I cannot argue with that, and I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly with Mr. Pavo Urban, again, have you read any of the transcript in relation to the circumstances of his body being found outside the Sponza palace under the clock tower in Dubrovnik, Old Town, on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, nothing apart from the medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I gave you a scenario before this Trial Chamber of Mr. Urban being seen wandering through the streets filming in the middle of shelling on the morning of the 6th of December while shells are landing in the Old Town, and then later that day being found struck down under the clock tower and brought to hospital, a man aged 26, with a wound, according to the forensic pathologist, being consistent with an explosive injury, would you accept there that that is also consistent with shelling causing shrapnel to fly into him being the cause of death? I'm sorry, I withdraw that. There's one other piece of information, and that is that Dr. Ciganovic in his evidence here which you haven't read said that at page 2747 "inside the abdomen I found a fragment and an explosive device that had caused the damage, and haemorrhage was the cause of death." If you take those three pieces of information, the photographer film being, the shelling, his body being found in the area where the shells had been landing, him being taken to the morgue, injury described, and the doctor saying in evidence that he found an explosive fragment which caused a haemorrhage. From that could you safely conclude that shelling was the thing that caused the shrapnel which caused the ultimate cause of death which was a haemorrhage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I believe that all these questions were about Pavo Urban. If you are asking me about Pavo Urban in the medical documentation prepared by the doctor, the cause of death is not indicated at all. As far as Pavo Urban is concerned, as far as I can see from the medical documentation, the cause of death is not stated. As for the rest, whether there was shelling or not, I cannot argue with that one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I appreciate it's not in the report, but if you take the extra piece of information from the doctor in evidence here, that he found inside Mr. Urban's body after doing a partial autopsy, that is opening it, a fragment, an explosive device, if you take that piece of information, combined with that, combined with the description of him walking around during the shelling and him being found dead there, you could safely conclude from that that the shelling had caused the shrapnel which had killed him by the haemorrhaging, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Please don't take exception. I cannot deny any of this. But it's not stated in the medical records. Maybe it was all the way you said it. My colleague did not describe it, however. As far as Pavo Urban is concerned, my colleague wrote that in the area of the naval. He found a wound about 5 centimetres in diameter, and injury to internal organs established or identified without postmortem. I cannot accept that, of course. The regulation is that the abdominal cavity has to be opened and injuries found inside described. I'm only a forensic pathologist, and I don't take anybody at their word. Forensic pathologists receive one set of information from the police, another from the postmortem, another set from the relatives, and that's what we operate with. I cannot take anybody at their word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic also asked you about bodies number 5 and number 7 which are in Dr. Ciganovic's report. And you've already referred to it in your own report which was filed here before. And you had some specific criticisms about some of the descriptions there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It must be about the unidentified bodies. If you mean the persons who remained unidentified, yes. If I understood you correctly -- yes, I had a critical comment because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to repeat. I'm just reminding you of where we were, of what your evidence was. Doctor, moving along, the last page of the report says that the pathologist Drago Kaleb has given information which is going to be checked, doesn't it? Authorised persons of the Dubrovnik police department will get all other necessary information, and so on. I don't want to read out the whole thing. But what it's indicating is that there's guess about who these two people are and that further inquiries have to be undertaken. That's what it's saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. And I didn't note it down. Yes. It's written there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you, of course, are unaware of the circumstances of these people being brought in, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: If it's not written in the medical record, then I cannot be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend would be so kind when talking about the record of examination, of external examination of Kaleb's, could he give the witness Exhibit P70 so that he has it in front of him before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything in front of me. I'm speaking from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. I saw the doctor referring to something. I presumed he had the exhibit there. Could he please be shown Exhibit P70.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have returned all of the documentation that had been given me. I had my own notes only. Yes, this is it. Yes, I've found that part, "authorised officers." I remember that part. Yes, yes, I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you don't know about the storage facilities in Dubrovnik morgue or hospital for bodies in December 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know whether DNA tests were done on these two bodies, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't seen photographs of them either, have you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know whether it would be possible to identify them from the photos, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No. If photographs were made, then today identification can be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've seen photographs of Mr. Skocko and Mr. Urban. It would be safe to assume that photos were taken of the other bodies, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It can be assumed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would accept that in circumstances where there has been -- where a number of people have been brought in dead, there are going to be relatives out there who are missing people? And they will probably come looking to see whether the unidentified bodies are those of their beloved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: They come, of course. They never fail to come. That's one way of identifying bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You accept if you look at this that the report is merely saying that the police should conduct further inquiries to properly ascertain the identity of the two persons whose names we think were Djuro Kolar and Ante Jablan. That's as far as it goes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that is police identification. That's not forensic identification. Forensic medical identification in this case is not sufficient, whereas police identification is another matter all together. It has nothing to do with Dr. Ciganovic. There are things that he should have done in order to keep some data for further identification of the bodies, for later identification, and he didn't do them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, on what basis can you possibly say that Dr. Ciganovic didn't keep items -- data for further identification of bodies if you have never been to Dubrovnik hospital, have no idea about the circumstances there, recordkeeping, storage of bodies, or what happened afterwards? How can you criticise Dr. Ciganovic if you didn't know what he did?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: If you remember, I didn't say that he hadn't done something. I said identification would be possible if he had kept certain parts or information in storage, like samples for DNA analysis. I didn't say that he didn't keep them. It didn't cross my mind to criticise him on that score. And I appreciate it very much if he has done his job properly. That's very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you just said, are you withdrawing what you said a moment ago? You said, "there are things he should have done in order to keep some data for further identification of the bodies for later identification, and he didn't do them." It's on the screen in front of you. Are you going to withdraw that piece of evidence now, that he didn't do the things he should have done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: When saying that, I meant the way he described things when -- during the external examination. I didn't mean to say that he hadn't kept samples or biological traces of body parts for later analysis. I meant say that he did not perform external examination in the way prescribed by forensic medicine. And I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber you were unaware of the conditions at Dubrovnik hospital in December 1991. Were you likewise unaware of conditions at Rijeka and Opatija in December, January, and February 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm completely unaware of that. The last time I spoke to my kums, kum relatives was in 1991. Kums who live in that part. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said a moment ago January and February 1991. I meant January and February 1992. I take it your answer referred to those months as well.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P211.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going from what you just said, you were unaware of the standard of recordkeeping at Dubrovnik hospital in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Of course I'm unaware of the recordkeeping as practiced in Dubrovnik in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also, I assume, unaware of the conditions in the hospital, not the pathology department, forensic pathology, but the hospital; that is, whether surgery was being performed, whether they had anaesthetics, whether they had proper supplies, whether they were fully equipped with staff, and you're unaware of the number of patients who were there and whether they were overcome with too many, aren't you, all of those things?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can only surmise if the war was going on that conditions had deteriorated there as elsewhere, indeed. But those are only assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you're unaware of the quality of the teaching or the quality of the recording of things in Latin at Dubrovnik hospital which, of course, depends on who does the recording, doesn't it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only provide an expert opinion on medical documentation. I know the rules of writing medical documentation. It has to be absolutely legible, and according to the rules of forensic medicine. Who did it there and under what conditions, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mistakes aren't unheard of in the recording of medical condition, are they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, a mistake is possible, that someone writes "right leg" instead of "left leg". That happens even in peacetime. It is not that much of a rarity. There is this kind of confusion between the two legs. But it is, nevertheless, a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at P211, the first page, now, that's a document with which you're familiar, that type of document? It's a register, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Registers, that's the word. Hospital registers, ward registers, that's the name we would refer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a big, big book in which someone writes in a very, very brief description of why the patient is there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who writes it in isn't necessarily a doctor, it could be a clerk or it could be a nurse, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to number C which is the specialist's note, that clearly refers to --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that clearly refers to the right leg, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That has been written by a person presumably had something to do with the operation, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's more likely to be accurate than the -- I'm sorry, if there's going to be inaccuracy, the inaccuracy is more likely to be in the register where someone else has written the details in than in the doctor's own report. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right. I believe the mistake was made by the surgeon rather than the administration clerk -- rather, that the administration clerk made a mistake rather than the surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could be satisfied on what you have read that it was the patient's right leg which was wounded, not his left leg?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume, too, that you haven't read Mr. Vlasica's testimony before this Tribunal in which he described receiving a wound to his upper right leg? You're unfamiliar with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that. I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I tell you that Mr. Vlasica described being in the street in Dubrovnik during the shelling, a shell detonating behind him, and him receiving an immediate wounding of his right leg which was severely bleeding and being taken to the hospital where he stayed for, I think, 11 days. When you put that piece of information together with the other things, all the other information there, you could safely conclude that he was wounded by shrapnel from a shell, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I can take your word for it or his word for it. But I, as a forensic expert, cannot make that kind of conclusion because I do not have that kind of information. I can only trust you, believe you, but as an expert before this Honourable Court, I cannot draw that kind of conclusion myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also -- just on the subject of the conditions and the quality of medical reporting, you're also unaware, I take it, that Mr. Vlasica was operated on by a doctor and two nurses without anaesthetics because he was told they were unavailable, and he was actually held down by two nurses with gauze between his teeth so as not to bite his tongue. You weren't aware of that either, were you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having heard that, does that put some of the things in perspective about the quality of care and recordkeeping at the Dubrovnik hospital in December 1991 during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: What you've said to me just now means that the conditions of work have been very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The left pulmonary top, that's in the lung area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right. It's the very top of the lungs underneath the collarbone area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P56. I've finished with P211.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to turn to the release form from Zagreb general -- Zagreb general hospital. Now, your evidence earlier today to the Tribunal was that you hadn't seen any documents in which shrapnel or a body, an alien body was described -- was described as being present in the lung area. I just want you to turn to the third or the fourth underlined heading, laboratory and other findings. Now, it says there "x-ray of heart and lungs without peculiarities. Alien body in the projection of the left pulmonary top. ECG without peculiarities." When you gave your evidence earlier that there was no -- nothing suggesting shrapnel in the lungs or the lung area, were you overlooking that particular finding from Zagreb general hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I am trying to follow you here as I read the translation into my mother tongue. And I am reading laboratory and other findings. And that's really what it says. Alien body in the projection of the left pulmonary top. This is an oversight on my part, but chest is a separate paragraph above, and there's no mention of it in that paragraph. The way I was taught in Zagreb precisely, that should have been in the paragraph that had to do with the chest. So I'm really sorry. It is indeed what is written here. "In the projection of the left pulmonary top," yes, there is a foreign body. I didn't notice that, I'm sorry. But I would have expected that to be written in the paragraph entitled "chest."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, I take it you haven't read Mr. Valjalo's testimony before the Tribunal in which he describes his various hospitalisation and visits to medical centres, and you're unaware of his evidence as to when particle -- or, when fragments of shrapnel were found in his body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I am not aware of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're unaware that Mr. Valjalo at page 2006 said "in Zagreb, they found another piece of shrapnel lodged in my lungs which I knew nothing about."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I don't know. All of that is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I just read to you from what he said is completely consistent with what is in the release form in the part I just referred to you about shrapnel -- an alien body in the projection of the left pulmonary top, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, you're also unaware of the previous page, page 2005, he described being x-rayed in Dubrovnik, and "I was on the table while they were x-raying me. They didn't operate. They did take out, extract certain fragments from my leg. Others remained lodged there. And they said they couldn't extract the one -- the other one because they were afraid of damaging me." And he was sent for further treatment in Rijeka. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that he had said that. But I see that after six days, he was sent from Dubrovnik to Rijeka. That can be seen from the medical records. But I'm not aware of his statement, his evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you accept everyone in the Court has heard that evidence being given and it's on the record here, that's what he said. If you accept that and the other piece of information about them finding the fragment in Zagreb, putting all of those pieces of -- putting those pieces of information together with the records provides the missing link and the consistency that you were looking for in his medical records, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: In all medical documents, reference is made to shrapnel. But only in the letter of discharge of the hospital in Rijeka there is mention of one removal of that foreign body from the neck area, whereas the rest refer to several foreign bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you put all those pieces of information together, him going to Dubrovnik with several pieces of shrapnel in him, some being taken out in Dubrovnik, another being removed in Rijeka, and then later on they -- discovering one in Zagreb, if you put all that together, that shows a consistency in relation to the shrapnel being in his body, doesn't it? All I'm saying is it basically overcomes your concerns if you put the two missing pieces of information in.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Certainly. In Zagreb, one was established in the lung, and Rijeka says neck area. So at least we have those two, according to this medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having looked at Mr. Valjalo's records and heard that information, if I tell you his evidence was that he was walking in the Stradun, a shell exploded close to him, and he fell to the ground wounded with injuries to his neck and his legs, that is consistent with what you've seen in the medical files, isn't it? A shell exploding about 40 to 50 metres away from him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, possibly, even from a 40-metre distance, part of shrapnel can end up in the head area or the neck area. I don't know where in the pulmonary top. I don't know where it went through. But Zagreb found it. All of that is possible. Only one is referred to unequivocally, though, and in Zagreb there is one that is referred to in the pulmonary top, and then there is the description of the chest, everything is normal, neurologically no peculiarities, and then this is found. So I have to take that. I have to accept that, that one was found in the lung tissue. That would mean two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm finished. I'm just checking with my colleague on one small detail, if you would just bear with me for one moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re. Mr. Rodic, do you think you'll be long?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Your Honour, approximately 20 minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that case, we'll have a break now, Mr. Rodic. And that will allow you to collect your thoughts. We'll resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Soc, in answer to one of the questions posed by my learned friend and colleague at one point you said that the working rules must be standard rules regardless of everything else. You referred to external circumstances such water and electricity and so on and so forth. First of all, tell me what does that mean that the rule must be the standard rule for everyone regardless of everything else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Excuse me.
