When I said that, what I had in mind was if you are about to start work on dead bodies, you must complete that job for as long as you are breathing and your health is not at risk, while you are still conscious. You can't skip things. You can't carry out an external examination by not including all 19 parameters in as long as that is possible, if your approach to your work is serious. I'm not sure if I'm making myself clear. You can't only use six parameters and not the remaining 12 or 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you P70, the record of external examination of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I've nothing in front of me right now. I only have my own notes that I have been dragging around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then have the usher's assistance, please, in providing these documents. I'm now talking about P70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have photographs there, too, P71 and P72 jointly? If not, can please the document be brought to you while I'm asking you the questions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, I don't see any photographs here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Soc, you saw the time that was recorded, between 9.15 and 3.00 p.m., so we calculate that this amounted to 3 hours and 45 minutes, didn't we, the entire time the work took?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also having inspected the photographs that you have been given now, you can see it, if you look at parts of the record, P70, you have seen that the bodies brought to the Dubrovnik hospital had clothing on, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also provided parameters in terms of the time frame, in terms much how long it takes in ideal conditions to carry out an external examination of a body, and you said it would take about 20 minutes, if I understand you correctly. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: You won't find this quoted anywhere in literature, the amount of time it takes. I based this estimate on my experience, and I think I've got quite some experience. And that would be the minimum it takes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please look at P70, the record. And just below the time when the examination started, it says "there are 19 dead bodies on the autopsy tables, persons who according to information that has been obtained were killed in the Dubrovnik town area and in the area of Sustjepan." It goes on to state in the next paragraph: "The crime technician is photographing the dead bodies. Having established the identities of each of the persons killed, the pathologist performs external examinations and establishes the cause of death." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of these 3 hours and 45 minutes, Dr. Soc, quite obviously the pathologists also identified the bodies because that's what the document states. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: What I see here is that, first of all, their identities were established, the bodies were identified, and then they proceeded to hand over the bodies to the pathologist for further processing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the individual items contained in this record in relation to each of the bodies, for example, under 11 in relation to Pavo Urban, the record reflects his birth, his place of residence, the place where he was allegedly killed, and the identity was established with the assistance of the following witnesses Pavo Djivanovic, his personal data, Vlaho Monkovic. Under 11, they identified the dead body as their friend Tonci Skocko. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the actions that a pathologist is supposed to perform when carrying out an external examination of a dead body, this work that was done between 9.15 and 3.00 p.m. also involved work done by crime technicians as well as work on identifying the dead bodies by persons who were present. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. It says "commencement at 9.15" and then they say they are beginning to identify the bodies, and then the inspection of the bodies, examination, and then the whole thing is supposed to finish at 3.00 p.m. That's at least what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, we are not making any assumptions here as speculating. This is the face of the document that you have in front of you. This work on identifying the bodies, would it also be included in this time frame which is defined as between 9.15 in the morning and 3.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That is also within that time frame because that's what the document states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned friend put to you the conditions that were in place in Dubrovnik at the time when these external examinations were performed. It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was not my intention to interrupt him, and I didn't. He told you that there was no running water, no electricity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir: Over a period of three months in Dubrovnik, October, November, and December 1991 specifically, if there is no running water, can people survive at all with no water for three months in a row?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, if I'm supposed to answer this question, I can only answer as an expert. In terms of how long a human being can go and maintain its normal bodily functions without water, as far as I remember, I think it should be about three days; without food for about seven days. And a normal human body can survive for about three days without water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you also said that under difficult working conditions, when an autopsy is performed -- rather, I apologise. I withdraw this question. Autopsies, that's a more complex procedure for a pathologist than a mere external examination, more complex in its nature?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, of course. When you perform an external examination, there is no contact with blood. An autopsy is a lot more complex, and you need to be much more skilled and trained. External examinations can be performed by doctors who are not specialists in forensic medicine. An autopsy, well, hardly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When faced with difficult working conditions, and my learned friend has spoken about these, at one point in time you said that bottled water could be used or would be sufficient. Can you please explain briefly why water is needed, what amounts of water are we looking at, and for what type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, nothing can be done. Well, what I had in mind when I said that in order to establish what the wounds are, first you need to wash the body the way it was brought in to the hall, the way you found the body when starting the autopsy. Then the performing pathologist is duty-bound to use with the help of his assistant, wash the body. If no poisoning is suspected, the body should be washed in order to spot all the changes, even the most minor changes on the body. The body must be washed in order to establish and discover these changes. There is another reason: When you rinse the internal organs when you look at the body, the contents of the internal organs, what's inside them, without water you just can't do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the term "bottled water" in order to carry out external examination of a dead body. How much water would you need for that, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I'm merely making an assumption here. I used a bucketful of water, perhaps a total of about 10 litres, for an entire autopsy. How much do you need? Well, as much as it takes to wash a body, the average height of which is 180 centimetres. I'm talking about the absolute minimum. We are looking at things here that under any normal circumstances would not be allowed at all, would be impermissible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question by my learned friend you said that the colleague of yours used to drive over from Montenegro to Dubrovnik prior to 1991. So what I want to know is what his profession was and what the reason was for him going to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It's Dr. Mihajlo Kulis. You know that I studied -- did my university studies in Zagreb, and I did my postgraduate studies in Zagreb as well. I had that information, and I know that Dr. Mihajlo Kulis regularly went to work on postmortems in Dubrovnik for the district court there because I had colleagues in Croatia, in Zagreb, in Split at the medical school. And he was one of my closest colleagues who had already studied -- who had also studied in Zagreb, but his main training is in forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you about is the reason why he went there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I can only assume. Podgorica is closer to Dubrovnik than Zagreb. There was no one closer to perform the work that needed to be performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was no specialist in forensic pathology in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, then, about blast injuries. Can they be inflicted even without shrapnel? Can they be induced by the explosion itself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: Well, there are certain injuries that can be sustained through the blast syndrome, the explosion itself can cause certain injuries that would qualify as blast injuries without the body being hit by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell us, how does one establish whether a bodily injury occurred while the person was still alive or posthumously?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: You cannot do that without performing a full postmortem. You can only have arbitrary assumptions. If you don't perform a postmortem and prove living reactions such as the flowing of blood in subcutaneous tissue, swallowing of blood, et cetera, you cannot -- you cannot claim that the person was still alive. You can only assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the record marked P70, from the description of wounds and injuries given in that record, can one assert with certainty whether these injuries occurred before or after death?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do object. There have been a number of questions that have been outside the scope of cross-examination. And in my submission, this one is. There was something my learned friend asked about in examination-in-chief and was answered. And I didn't go into it in cross-examination. It's merely repetition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think asking about when certain injuries occurred is outside of re-examination, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'll explain. The purpose of my questioning is to elucidate entries into the record. I want the doctor as an expert in forensic pathology to comment on them because my colleague presented him with photographs during proofing. A shell fell here, somebody says that somebody was injured here. It was wartime. The person could already have been dead before the shell landed. And the body could have sustained injuries other than from the shell. I'm just asking whether from this description of injuries, it is possible to give an opinion based on such description as to whether the injuries were sustained before or after death. It is a matter for expertise of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be that, Mr. Rodic, but the question is whether it's properly now raised in re-examination. As it's Wednesday afternoon, if you ask the question quickly and get an answer quickly, we'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the doctor can give us a brief and quick answer because he is very experienced. May I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on external examination, one cannot speak of the cause or mechanism of death. One cannot determine the cause of death. And that means that we cannot say whether it was before or after death that injury was sustained. I brought a book here that says "it is quite certain that based on an external examination or even partial postmortem, the cause of death cannot be determined definitively."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness speaks too fast for us to follow such important subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During my examination-in-chief, I presented you with a number of documents, for instance, item 5 that mentions a small piece of shrapnel in the upper arm. In both cases, is there any mention of foreign body, be it shrapnel, projectile, bullet, et cetera, in this P70 record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I haven't found it. I haven't found any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you while describing the testimony of Dr. Ciganovic from the medical centre, the author of that record who had testified previously before the Trial Chamber, when he explained in part how he performed the postmortems or how he performed partial postmortems. Under this term "partial postmortem," as used in this P70 record, can we see that even this partial postmortem was done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I only found in this text that a lot of blood was found in the abdominal cavity and in the chest, but there is no such term as "partial postmortem." Only an uneducated person can use it. It is absolutely inappropriate. Certain partial procedures are performed, even I perform them depending on the circumstances. But this is highly irregular and contrary to the rules of the profession. No conclusions can be drawn from it. Anybody who would draw such conclusions would be wrong and out of line professionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to know, even if we assume that such partial postmortem was done, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let me finish. In one part of this record, you said you found blood in the abdominal cavity. My question related to this is the following: In the record P70, can one see that Dr. Ciganovic had performed or rather had written that he had performed a single incision on the bodies he had examined? Is there any record of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I haven't found any such entry anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 11 of the record, P70, referring to Tonci Skocko --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere here that the wound was reconstructed, which implies incision, expanding, or deepening of the wound?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: It is not written there. The only thing that's written is that a 13-millimetre wound was found. There is a description of its location as well as the channel. And only based on external examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at number 15, Pavo Urban. Do we see any trace here of the pathologist's work in the form of incisions made on the cadaver?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, there are none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 15 relating to Pavo Urban, is there any information that the pathologist had found a shrapnel or bullet lodged in the body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, would a professional pathologist be amiss in failing to enter in the record that he had found such a thing, a shrapnel or bullet?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. This is merely repetition of the examination-in-chief. The doctor -- the good doctor has criticised at length in his filed report, Dr. Ciganovic's report, did so again in examination-in-chief. This is merely repetition. And the last few questions have in my submission really been more in the nature of a submission. The record does speak for itself, and my learned friend is entitled to submit at the end of the day what the report says or doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have got to say, Mr. Rodic, that I see nothing new in any of this. It's really just trying to pull all that the doctor gave in evidence earlier together in a summary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The subject of expertise of this witness was only the medical documentation given to him. No records of testimony before this Trial Chamber, no transcripts were included. This witness spent most of the examination-in-chief presenting quotations from the -- sorry, my learned friend spent most of the cross-examination putting to the witness parts of the transcripts of the witnesses. And Mr. Ciganovic said at one point that 13 years later he remembered that during external examination of the body of late Pavo Urban, he had found shrapnel in his body. My learned friend just mentioned it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I agree with all of that. But what you are doing with the witness now in a series of questions and answers is merely putting to him again the evidence that he gave originally. That evidence stands. So this is entirely unnecessary repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Soc, tell me briefly, according to the rules of your profession governing records, or rather entries into the record of descriptions and findings made during postmortem, would absence or lack of water be a hinderance? Would it prevent you from making entries into the record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: In order to write something down, I need water.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction. Answer: I would write down that there was no water available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Soc, do you know whether in Dubrovnik on the 7th of December there was any shelling or fighting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time, I was undergoing specialisation in Belgrade. All I know is what I heard from the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Soc, in the course of reviewing the medical documentation for Ivo Vlasica, that is, by studying his medical file including this last piece of evidence presented to you, P211, that is the medical protocol and the case history, were you able to draw the conclusion that according to the medical documentation, Ivo Vlasica had been wounded in the right or left leg?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: No, I could only assume. I would have to trust either my colleague the surgeon or chalk it down to an error in order to decide which leg it was. I would have to trust my colleague, the surgeon. And I decided to trust the surgeon. But I could not draw the conclusion whether it was the right or the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, as a specialist in forensic pathology and a forensic examiner, based on this medical documentation, can you tell precisely which of his legs was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I still abide by my opinion formed earlier that I don't know which leg it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, regarding Ivo Vlasica, when you have the complete medical documentation in front of you, are you able to say whether Ivo Vlasica was injured by shrapnel or projectile or something else yet? Could you form a definitive opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I included in my report, among other things, that it was a sclopetaria wound. I don't know what caused this gunshot wound based on the medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When looking at Exhibit P211, namely, this protocol and the case history, the finding of the specialist as well as the x-ray report and opinion, is there any reference to any surgery done on Ivo Vlasica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SOC
utterances.text: I haven't found any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Soc. Your Honour, I have concluded the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. Doctor, may the Tribunal thank you for your assistance and for the time you've taken to give evidence here. You'll be pleased to know that you're now free to return to your home and work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an honour for me to take part in the proceedings of The Hague Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to introduce yourself to the Honourable Trial Chamber with your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I'm Ludvik Renko, born on the 5th of May 1933 in Lokve near Nova Gorica, at that time in fascist Italy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, could you please tell us what your current profession Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me when you retired?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: On the 1st of January 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you retired with a particular rank?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: The rank of lieutenant colonel in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were an active-duty officer?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, could you please tell us what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Slovene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what citizenship do you have?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Currently of Slovenia. Before that, of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you live.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I live in Ljubljana. That's where my registered domicile is. But I live in Lokve near Nova Gorica. I come to Ljubljana every now and then when necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what post did you hold when you retired?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I was retired from the position of a member of the operations department of the 9th Army as an officer for property and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, I will have to ask you something. For the transcript, all this is being interpreted. Could you please pause briefly after I put my question so that everything could be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, which military schools did you complete?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: This is the way it was: With Mr. Strugar, I completed the three-year military academy. After that, I finished a one-year school, an additional school, and the political school of the JNA which also lasted one year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where did you attend the military academy?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: The military academy, this is the way it was: At that time, the then-General Staff of the JNA proclaimed that civilians may be enrolled in military schools. And then I applied. Because until then, there weren't any active-duty officers in the JNA who had been civilians before that. There were only wartime officers in the officers corps until then. So I applied and I was accepted. And in 1949, in the month of September, I came at that Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Renko, tell me, please, during your active-duty military service, in which garrisons did you serve?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Upon completing my education as a lieutenant, first I served in Koprivnica, in the border regiment near Hungary. Then I was in Lendava, in the border units, in the Gornji Petrovci in the border units. Then -- Gornji Petrovci, let me think, then Baranjsko Petrovo Selo in Banat, in the border units. Or Rather, this was in Beli Manastir. I was transferred from there to Skofja Loka, to the mountain brigade. And that was the first time I saw Mr. Strugar again after our school years. Then, in 1968, when the Warsaw Pact powers entered Czechoslovakia, then I was transferred to Maribor urgently. And then from Maribor, four years later, I was transferred to Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What rank did you hold after you completed military academy?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what post did you hold in Skofja Loka?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: In Skofja Loka I was company commander there, and for a while I was deputy commander of the garrison itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know Mr. Strugar well?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I know him extremely well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you met him.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: We met, it was the end of September 1949 in Kragujevac. As I said earlier on, we had applied and were admitted to the school. We were students from all parts of the former Yugoslavia, from all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. At that time, there were nine of us Slovenes, and we were in different platoons and companies. So in every platoon, there was approximately one Slovene respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. Were you together in that platoon?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to tell you right now. I'm taking things in the right order. So, once we were there, there were about 30 of us in this platoon, and there were three squads. In the first squad, I was together with Mr. Strugar immediately. We were assigned to the same squad, the same platoon, from day one until the end of our schooling. That was the 3rd of August 1952.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Renko, we have very little time available, so could you please tell us briefly under which conditions your schooling took place, yours and Mr. Strugar's.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: It is well known that then -- the then Yugoslavia was in a very difficult economic and political situation. So that had an effect on us military cadets; that is to say, we did not have what cadets have nowadays at different military academies. We were modest. We had modest food and a firm discipline. It was some kind of a mix between the former Yugoslav and Russian discipline until this system of discipline was not built later on in the JNA. That's what I mean. It was very strenuous because our average age ranged between 16 and 17. That was 70 per cent of us. And there were a few who were even younger than that. At that time, for us, this was physically a tremendous strain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that the discipline in that school was strict.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Strict, yes. And I think that this discipline led to our formation as human beings, the firmness of our characters. We -- instead of going to school during the war, we had to flee. I also had to flee from my home because the Germans in 1943 burned down my home and my village and my school. So there were many cadets who did not have one parent or both parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the constitution of General Strugar at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He was a head above all of us at the time, he was taller than all of us at that time. And that's why he headed the squad at that time. But Strugar was the first leader of that squad. He was a head above all of us, he was taller than all of us. So he was our first squad leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he help you any in that period?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes. Since I did not know Serbo-Croat at the time when I arrived, I went to high school for four years and I learned some at that time. But that was very little. And he helped me with pronunciation first and foremost, although I did not get rid of that pronunciation until the present day really. So he always corrected me. And then this friendly relationship that we had and generally everybody in the squad, not only he and I, we practically had no problems. Further on, he helped me. I remember on this march between Kraljevo and Kragujevac. He was a head taller than I was, and he was strong, and he helped me, and he even carried my rifle. There were so many other things he did. You cannot remember all the things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Renko, how would you describe General Strugar's personality?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: First and foremost, how should I put this? General Strugar is a firm personality by his very nature. Also, he is a humane person. He likes to help people in a friendly way. He empathises with people, listens to people's troubles. And I think that he made a lot of friends everywhere precisely because of that. Further on, I can claim with 100 per cent certainty that he was not a nationalist or chauvinist. He respected members of all different ethnic groups. He didn't really pay attention to that kind of thing, I'm a Serb, I'm Montenegrin or whatever. He has none of that in him. Just like I don't. Just like I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He does not have that in him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how do you know him? Was he quarrelsome? Was he an angry person?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I never saw the man angry, ever. Perhaps this may seem a bit abstract. But instead of getting angry, he would smile or laugh. That is characteristic of him. I remember once, I remember very well when we were joking about, and somebody insulted him a bit, but he was not offended. He even laughed. And I even said to him, I said, how can you take it, that kind of insult? I mean, it was a boy thing, but anyway...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said that among the cadets there were members of all different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Strugar's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He's an ethnic Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his option, what had he opted for?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: What do you mean "option"? He had a general Yugoslav orientation. He was an all-Yugoslav person. We socialised, and he would never manifest any such thing, Montenegrins, whatever. Of course, sometimes I would see a Slovene within the compound and exchange a few words, and he would do the same thing with Montenegrins. Let me tell you, this generation of mine, my year, my class, we were not corrupt. How can I put this? We were not poisoned with nationalism, chauvinism, and racism. You see what I mean? This is a class that has stuck together until the present day. We still meet up. Two years ago we had a meeting, a reunion, in Belgrade. We have our own newsletter which comes out twice a year. We are scattered about all the newly established states, but still we maintain these ties. This class of mine, I'm talking about my class, was the soundest or healthiest of all with regard to that particular matter, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, can you tell us something about the moral standards, the values of Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: As I said, he is a man with very high moral values such as every human being should have, if you understand what I'm saying. As an officer and as a soldier, I trust he has shown by his example as an officer to be a just man. He required a lot of discipline and he required order. That's clear enough. But he had that moral backbone, and he had a strength of character to listen to each of his subordinates and that's why people held him in high esteem. He would look at his subordinates and he would say, If I have no respect for my subordinates, then my unit is weak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about General Strugar's family background? What sort of family does he come from?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He is from a worker's family from Pec. Most of us came from rural and working backgrounds at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Strugar family, did they take part in the national struggle in World War II?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I don't know all of their names by heart. But I know that his uncles had taken part in the struggle against fascism. That was one thing that was typical of my generation, of my class. We all had relatives who had fought against the fascists. It was a generation of people who all had relatives who had fought in World War II against the fascists, the war of national liberation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, and based on your experience with Mr. Strugar, did he have a big talent for being in the army, for becoming an officer? Was he talented?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He was a natural soldier, I tell you. It was easy to see from day one at the academy. He was a joyful person, just as I was, and he enjoyed this career, this profession. You must enjoy your career. It's the key to success. And that is why he has come this far. He didn't come this far because someone happened to like him. He had to work hard for it. In addition to all other qualities that Mr. Strugar had, the way his units behaved during his service was particularly characteristic. And then it goes without saying, you need to have the right qualifications, the level of training, educational background. If you have the former without the latter, there's no way you can ever attain the rank of lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Strugar work in the same unit for a while?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that was back in 1964. I think that was the first time we saw each other later. I think in 1964 was the first time we were reunited. He worked as garrison commander in Bolovac [phoen], and I was in Skofja Loka at the time. We first saw each other at a military exercise, a session. Due to the distance separating our two garrisons, we were not in touch every month or every week, but there would be meetings in Tomijn [phoen], and we would meet up there. There was this once when we took part in a military exercise together. At Bovec, I had arrived from my unit own at Skofja Loka, and we did that military exercise together for a stretch of eight days, those manoeuvres that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Strugar's units rate?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: He had the best battalion in the mountain brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he deserve to become general? Did he deserve the rank that he held in as far as you can say?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent without a question. He's a modest man. He is not overly ambitious, not in the wrong way. He earned whatever he obtained. It wasn't because someone happened to like him. And it wasn't to the detriment of one of his subordinates. He worked hard for it, and he earned everything he got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he pursued any specialised courses?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes, he completed all the possible military schools that were available in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name a typical example of how General Strugar cared.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I still remember after so many years the military exercise that I referred to. We were together then. And there was a soldier in one of his units who had been imprisoned for ten years. He was some sort of a criminal, a murderer. By the time he met Strugar, he was 28 years old. I believed he hailed from Kragujevac. His name was Dimic or Djimic or something like that. And he was assigned to my unit. He had to cross the mountain, and this soldier talked to me. He was a bit of a strange person. He hated people. I'm not sure how that could ever be, but he simply hated other people. And he wanted Strugar or another officer to give him a horse because the horse was his best friend back there at Bovec. And that's what he told me after he had been assigned to my unit. And I know because I talked to him at the time. He said "I tried talking to him the nice way as his commander in order to try to show this man the way, get him to stop hating other people or other soldiers who were there." He was surrounded by other people after all. And this was an example which showed his concern, his care for individual soldiers, not to mention officers. The garrison as far as I know was far away from a big town. It was isolated. People needed to help each other. People needed helping out. And Strugar was always the first, the officer that was really held in high esteem and that everyone relied upon when they needed help. And allow me to finish, please. There was once a celebration, a festivity, years later, and I asked him about that particular soldier, and Strugar told me "well, he remained the same, he never changed" meaning that he had not managed to accomplish anything with that particular soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, are you still friends with Mr. Strugar?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Well, if you like, I have a photograph on me which I can show you to prove that dated the 4th of October 2002, Belgrade, a celebration we had. I must give him the photograph today because I have still not had an opportunity to give him these photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still hold General Strugar in the highest possible esteem as an officer and a person?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: I have no second thoughts at all about this. He couldn't have done anything wrong. He's just not that kind of person. He's not a person who could possibly hurt anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've known him for a very long time. Have you ever heard people say anything bad about General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No, never. The only thing, maybe now I read something in the public media down there, whatever happened, the evil thing that happened down there. But I know of nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, let me ask you this: Do you know that General Strugar was the first general of the JNA to voluntarily surrender to the ICTY, of his own free will, that is?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: That's one thing I was about to say. The question I would like to ask is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's leading. Let the witness answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is leading, but it is a character witness. Carry on, Mr. Rodic, could I make the point, though, that we are told that the witness needs to leave The Hague tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll just take another minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for leaving The Hague, the administration has failed to make the appropriate arrangements because I had to pay for my own air ticket from Ljubljana, and until these things are cleared up, I'll be staying for at least another day. Therefore, the time issue is not really an issue at all. There's no plane that I need to take tonight. If I'm doing something for Mr. Strugar, I'm prepared to go a very long way I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Renko.

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: There was another thing I needed to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, would you just listen to Mr. Rodic and answer his questions, please. It will be a lot better for General Strugar and everybody else if you do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honour. I fully accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, did you hear yourself that General Strugar surrendered of his own free will to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes. And I have a cutting from one of the newspapers at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Well, he was a conscientious man, and he felt not guilty. Any one who felt guilt at the time would have tried to escape. It's just human nature. If you're hiding, if you're telling lies, that means you feel guilty. You do anything to escape the tension and escape being brought to justice. That is why I think that what he did was an honest and honourable thing to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there something that I didn't ask you, something that's brief and that you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: There is something that I would like to say, but you interrupted me. First of all, I came of my own free will to testify before this Court because General Strugar is my friend, my colleague. We have known each other for 55 years. I felt I had a moral responsibility towards him and his family. And that's why I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Renko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Weiner, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: L be very brief. Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Philip Weiner. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to be brief. It won't be very long. About a -- two minutes ago you said, "that evil thing that happened down there," when you were testifying. When you referred to the evil thing, you were referring to the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you weren't with General Strugar on December 6th, 1991 while he was the commander of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not a witness --

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not a witness to what he said or did there at that time?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nor are you a witness --

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to what he said after December 6th in the next two months as commander of the 2nd Operational Group in relation to the Old Town of Dubrovnik? You're not a witness to what he said or did, what actions he took?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And further, you're not a witness to any actions he took in October or November of 1991 in relation to the Old Town of Dubrovnik or in relation to the 2nd operation command?

utterances.speaker: LUDVIK RENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not really, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Renko, I'm happy to tell you that your evidence here is concluded. May we thank you for your assistance. I'm sure that your friend and colleague, the accused, would thank you deeply as well. And I wish you luck with the administration tomorrow. You are free to return to your home when you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. But this may be a good opportunity. I'm not sure if I have your permission. Do you think we could have your permission for General Strugar to greet and shake hands with Mr. Renko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When the Chamber has left the Court, if they came close together over there for a few moments, I'm sure the security people will be able to cope with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
